#9934. Go Turns 17

Stories about how and why companies use Go

How Go can help keep you secure by default

A complete introduction to building software with Go

Reference documentation for Go's standard library

Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code

Learn and network with Go developers from around the world

Austin Clements, for the Go team 10 November 2026

Today, November 10th, we celebrate the 17th anniversary of Go’s open source release!

Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our golang.org/x libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility, while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a dual purpose: what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective.

In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world experience. When generics first landed in Go 1.18, methods could not declare their own type parameters, which sometimes forced awkward package-level functions and “inside-out” nested calls. Go 1.27 introduced generic methods on non-interface types (such as the new Rand.N method in math/rand/v2), allowing APIs to stay naturally organized on types and enabling readable method chaining. Together with support for self-referential type constraints in Go 1.26 and broader type inference for generic function values in Go 1.27, generics in Go feel more complete and natural than ever.

Alongside generics, two refinements to value construction make everyday Go code cleaner and more concise. Go 1.26 extended the built-in new function to accept an initial value expression, allowing new(42) or new("go1.26") without the ubiquitous newInt-style helper functions used to populate optional pointer fields in JSON and protocol buffer structs. And in Go 1.27, struct literal keys can refer directly to fields of embedded or nested structs, reducing boilerplate in composite literals.

In the standard library, our focus has been on evolving Go’s “production stack” and eliminating subtle operational traps. Few packages are as central to that as encoding/json, which has been a mainstay of Go since before Go 1.0. While its core model has held up remarkably well for over 15 years, tighter JSON standards and security expectations have turned some of its original defaults into interoperability and security hazards, such as silently accepting invalid UTF-8 or duplicate object keys and matching struct fields case-insensitively. At the same time, its buffered design prevented true streaming and limited performance. Addressing these issues while upholding Go’s compatibility promise for the millions of existing programs that depend on encoding/json meant designing a new major version of the package.

Six years in the making, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages reached general availability in Go 1.27. Driven by Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, and contributors from across the Go community, this modern JSON API brings safer, stricter defaults, flexible caller- and type-specified customization, and up to 10× faster unmarshaling, while cleanly separating high-level semantic marshaling (json/v2) from low-level, reflection-free syntactic streaming (jsontext). Crucially, we didn’t leave existing code behind: the original encoding/json package is now implemented entirely in terms of v2 under the hood. Existing v1 callers get faster unmarshaling simply by upgrading, and packages using v1 and v2 interoperate seamlessly so that the ecosystem can migrate gradually without flag days.

We’ve also brought new production diagnostics to Go’s concurrency primitives. Concurrency is one of Go’s greatest strengths, but goroutines accidentally left blocked on abandoned channels or locks can silently leak memory and CPU in long-running services, and traditional goroutine profiles cannot distinguish leaked goroutines from ones legitimately waiting for work. First previewed in Go 1.26 and now generally available in Go 1.27, the new goroutine leak profiler (goroutineleak in runtime/pprof and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof) solves this for production services. Contributed by Vlad Saioc and Uber’s Programming Systems team, building on academic research with Aarhus University and Washington University in St. Louis, the profiler repurposes the garbage collector’s reachability phase to identify goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives that no runnable goroutine can ever reach. That allows it to pinpoint leaks in production with near-zero false positives and zero overhead when not in use.

In net/http, closing an HTTP/1 response body with even a single unread byte—such as a trailing newline left behind by a JSON decoder—previously forced the client to tear down the underlying TCP and TLS connection. Go 1.27’s HTTP transport now automatically drains small unread response bodies in the background on close, turning a widespread latency footgun into up to a 5× speedup for sequential HTTP/1 requests while letting application code stay clean and simple.

These releases also added several notable standard library APIs, including a native uuid package, a generic and type-safe errors.AsType, and an in-memory httptest.NewTestServer designed for virtual-time testing with testing/synctest. Existing packages saw significant speedups as well: io.ReadAll now runs twice as fast while allocating half as much memory, compress/flate compresses faster (speeding up gzip, zip, zlib, and png), and image/jpeg has a faster, more accurate encoder and decoder.

Modern CPUs look very different from the hardware Go first launched on 17 years ago, with wide vector units and deep, non-uniform memory hierarchies. A major focus of our runtime and compiler work is ensuring Go programs make full use of modern silicon, both transparently when you upgrade your toolchain and through new APIs when you need explicit control.

After debuting as an experiment in Go 1.25, the Green Tea garbage collector became the default in Go 1.26. By organizing object marking around contiguous memory spans rather than chasing pointers across the heap, Green Tea aligns with modern CPU memory architectures to reduce garbage collection overhead by 10–40% in real-world workloads—and by an additional ~10% on recent amd64 processors using AVX-512 vector instructions during scanning.

Of course, the runtime shouldn’t be the only part of a Go program that can tap into vector hardware. Without access to Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) capabilities, compute-intensive software, from cryptography and media processing to data analytics and AI, leaves a significant portion of modern silicon dark. Until recently, the only way to light up that hardware in Go was by writing and maintaining per-architecture assembly. To change that, Go 1.26 and 1.27 introduced two experimental SIMD packages: simd/archsimd, for low-level access to architecture-specific vector instructions on amd64, arm64 (NEON), and WebAssembly (wasm); and simd, a higher-level, width-agnostic API that provides portable, near-assembly performance across architectures with automatic fallback emulation.

We’ve also attacked the cost of memory allocation from multiple angles. The cheapest heap allocation is the one that never happens: in Go 1.26, the compiler began allocating initial slice backing stores on the stack at append sites—even for slices that ultimately escape to the heap—eliminating the flurry of small heap allocations that typically accompany slice growth. And for heap allocations more broadly, Go 1.27 introduced size-specialized memory allocation to speed up allocating the small objects (such as small structs, slices, and strings) that dominate allocator time. Generating dedicated fast-path allocator routines for size classes up to 80 bytes made small allocations up to 30% faster and improved overall performance in allocation-heavy programs. Together with a ~30% reduction in baseline cgo call overhead in Go 1.26, these improvements make Go programs faster and leaner out of the box.

Go’s approach to security spans the entire lifecycle of software: providing safe APIs by design, preparing cryptography for the future, and actively defending the live ecosystem as new threats emerge.

To defend against store-now, decrypt-later attacks and support the industry’s accelerating timelines for quantum readiness, Go has continued expanding its post-quantum cryptography support. Go 1.26 enabled hybrid post-quantum key exchanges (SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024) by default in crypto/tls and added the crypto/hpke package (implementing RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption, including post-quantum hybrid KEMs). Go 1.27 followed up with the new crypto/mldsa package, implementing the FIPS 204 post-quantum ML-DSA signature standard and integrating it into crypto/x509 and crypto/tls.

At the same time, we’ve continued hardening the standard library and runtime against subtle classes of vulnerabilities. Most key generation and signing functions across Go’s crypto/... packages now unconditionally draw from a secure system randomness source, closing off a classic footgun where non-cryptographic readers were accidentally passed in. Under the hood, Go 1.26 also added 64-bit heap base address randomization to harden cgo binaries and introduced the experimental runtime/secret package for eagerly erasing sensitive cryptographic temporaries from registers, stack frames, and the heap.

Securing Go deployments also requires rapid vulnerability and incident response in a fast-moving threat landscape. From the Go vulnerability database and govulncheck to our release infrastructure, we’ve invested heavily in ecosystem defense. In October, that preparation was put to the test during the eMudhra certificate key disclosure incident, when eight intermediate TLS and code-signing certificates chaining to a widely trusted root CA were discovered to use trivially weak private keys. Because Linux lacks a uniform OS-level certificate revocation mechanism, Go’s built-in TLS verifier is the frontline defense for millions of Linux services. Within seven and a half hours of initial notification, the Go Security team shipped a targeted block in our first-ever URGENT track security release (Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10) alongside an updated Go vulnerability database entry so govulncheck could flag affected binaries, giving Go users everything they needed to protect their deployments before the weak keys were publicly disclosed the next morning.

Go has always been more than a compiler and standard library: it is an end-to-end platform for software engineering. Over the past year, our work in golang.org/x/tools, the gopls language server, vscode-go, and pkg.go.dev has focused on making that platform even more productive for both human developers and AI coding assistants.

In last fall’s Go Developer Survey, the single biggest challenge developers reported was ensuring their code follows best practices and current Go idioms. As Go evolves while standing by its compatibility promise, older ways of writing code continue to work alongside newer, clearer, or faster alternatives, creating a natural drift in idioms over time. That drift has been compounded by AI coding assistants, which gravitate toward the older patterns that dominate their training data.

Go 1.26 tackled this with a complete overhaul of the go fix command, returning the long-dormant tool to its pre-Go 1.0 roots to apply dozens of automatic modernizers across entire codebases. What gofmt did for stylistic consistency, modernizers aim to do for idiomatic consistency. Available both as instant suggestions in gopls and as bulk, push-button upgrades in go fix, modernizers simplify existing code and help developers discover new language and library features. We now routinely consider whether new language and library proposals should ship with a modernizer of their own. Just as importantly, modernizers give coding agents an immediate way to bring generated code up to date, while helping shift the global corpus of open source Go code so that future models learn modern idioms from the start.

Bespoke modernizers work well for the language and standard library, but a centralized team can never write them for every third-party module in the ecosystem. That’s why Go 1.26 also introduced the annotation-driven source-level inliner, the first step toward a “self-service” paradigm for automated code maintenance. Any package author can now annotate a deprecated function, type, or constant with //go:fix inline, and the inliner will safely migrate callers and references via go fix or in the IDE, carefully handling evaluation order, side effects, and name shadowing.

In the editor, we’ve made four feature-packed releases of gopls over the past year (v0.21.0, v0.22.0, v0.23.0, and v0.24.0). In collaboration with the Dart team, we designed and proposed an open Language Server Protocol (LSP) extension for interactive refactoring, allowing language servers to ask for user input through dynamic, multi-step dialogs in any supporting editor. Now integrated into gopls and vscode-go, interactive refactoring powers customizable struct tag addition and removal, interface implementation (including generic interfaces) with live symbol search, and cross-package declaration moves. Beyond refactoring, gopls also gained generalized package renaming across directories, zero-configuration support for editing Go assembly files, subexpression hover inspection, completions and inlay hints for promoted fields, automatic govulncheck scanning when go.mod dependencies change, and continued enhancements to its built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI coding assistants.

Rounding out the developer platform, in May we launched the official pkg.go.dev API and followed up with support for go doc pkg@version in Go 1.27. Previously, developer tools and IDE integrations had to resort to fragile web scraping to query ecosystem metadata. Today, the pkg.go.dev API gives tool authors and AI coding agents a fast, authoritative service for querying module versions, package symbols, importers, and vulnerability data, while go doc pkg@version makes it easy to pull up documentation for any version of any package right from the command line.

On the tooling front, we’re building on the pkg.go.dev API, gopls, and go fix to make Go’s developer tools even more capable for both human developers and coding agents. Following the strong community response to go fix and //go:fix inline, we’re exploring ways to expand self-service static analysis, enabling developers, package maintainers, and organizations to easily integrate custom analyzers and domain-specific best-practice checks directly into their development workflows. We’re also exploring ways to surface richer package health and quality signals on pkg.go.dev and through its API, helping developers and coding agents evaluate and choose trustworthy, reliable dependencies.

In the language and libraries, Go 1.28 will resolve one of Go’s longest-standing language requests by allowing composite literals to omit redundant types whenever the type can be inferred from context, cutting visual noise in deeply nested configurations, API requests, and table-driven tests. And with recent generics refinements and hashing APIs in place, we’ve just accepted a swath of proposals for generic collection APIs—including sets, ordered maps, and more—which will land in golang.org/x/exp over the next few weeks so the community can try them out and share feedback ahead of future standard library inclusion.

Under the hood, we’re working hard to graduate a large subset of the simd and simd/archsimd packages (covering amd64, arm64 NEON, and wasm) in Go 1.28, with further expansions and arm64 scalable vector (SVE) support targeted for Go 1.29. Amid the global RAM crunch, reducing Go’s memory footprint is also one of our major priorities for the coming year.

In the toolchain, Go 1.28 will increase build parallelism by writing compiler export data early and streamline static analysis by decoupling tool export data from the compiler. Looking further out, we’re working to support cgo builds without requiring a C toolchain, and we’re kicking the tires on WebAssembly’s early-stage stack-switching extension, which is already showing promising improvements in Go Wasm performance and binary size.

Finally, ensuring Go stands the test of time means scaling not just our technology, but the open source project itself. Over the past year, some of Go’s most impactful advances, including encoding/json/v2 and the goroutineleak profile, were driven by or built in close partnership with contributors outside Google. To better support our growing ecosystem and contributor base, we’re working to bridge the gap between Go maintainers at Google and our broader community, and to diversify Go’s technical stewardship. That includes restructuring the proposal process to improve throughput, give the community clearer visibility into the process and input into prioritization, and formally involve community contributors in triage and review. Beyond proposals, we are building a clearer contributor ladder to empower proven contributors with greater autonomy, decision-making privileges, and maintenance responsibilities, and opening up maintainer summits and day-to-day communications to trusted contributors from our amazing community.

Seventeen years in, Go is thriving because of the people who use it, build with it, and contribute to it every day. Thank you to everyone in the Go community for being part of this journey, and we wish you all the best in the year ahead!

#9933. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9932. Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python

Newly open sourced XSE handles six million queries a second across services including Search, Ads, and YouTube Shorts

"Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work.

Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors.

The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE, short for the XLA Serving Engine.

XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google.

"LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach, Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday.

At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search.

These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing.

A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory.

In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel."

Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here.

XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators.

Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML community. Beyond XSE, other approaches have been taken, many of which involve jettisoning the Python code as quickly as possible. PyTorch offers a native C++ runtime called LibTorch. Also, Microsoft and its collaborators offer the ONNX Runtime, which supports an open graph format with Python bindings.

Even Python's own reference implementation relies heavily on C, with Rust now getting a foot in the door. ®

#9931. The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English

Benchmarks decide what gets built. A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve. Much of the recent work on the leaderboard has gone into making the evaluation metrics more trustworthy:

All of that makes one number (WER) harder to game. It is still one number. A long line of work has shown that ASR error rates are not evenly distributed across the people using them. Racial disparities in automated speech recognition found commercial systems roughly twice as bad for Black speakers as for white speakers, and Quantifying Bias in Automatic Speech Recognition found further differences by gender, age and accent. None of that is visible on a leaderboard, and not because the leaderboard is hiding it. The test sets it runs on record what was said and almost nothing about who said it.

To address this gap, we introduce two evaluation sets to the Open ASR Leaderboard: Monsoon en-IN and Monsoon hi-IN. Hindi, spoken by more than half a billion people, is the first Indic language on a multilingual tab that currently covers only European languages. Each set is released as a public split, available for self-scoring, and a private split withheld to limit benchmark-specific optimisation. The four splits are speaker-disjoint, comprising 4,888 speakers, with 12 speaker attributes recorded for each.

A test set can only expose a failure mode it varies along. Most benchmarks are built from whatever audio was readily available. Monsoon was built to vary along nine axes: geography, age, gender, vocabulary, devices, acoustic environments, speech type, speech rate, and the existence of multiple valid transcripts for the same audio. Each is a way an aggregate WER can be right on average and wrong for a particular population.

Four splits, two languages, collected through one pipeline.

The data is sourced from unscripted dual-channel spontaneous conversations, with clips segmented from a single channel so that each clip carries one speaker. Along with the fields reported in the table, each clip also records occupation, education, marital status, income band, handset brand, current city and years in the current district.

Five clips from the public Indian English split, with the metadata each one carries:

29-year-old woman, West Tripura, Tripura. Student, samsung SM-G781B.

32-year-old woman, Satna, Madhya Pradesh. Unemployed, samsung SM-E146B.

22-year-old man, Rohtas, Bihar. Student, motorola moto g54 5G.

27-year-old woman, Warangal, Telangana. Unemployed, vivo V2247.

57-year-old man, Puducherry. Private job, Xiaomi M2006C3LI.

The English sets use standard string references, where the leaderboard's normaliser collapses most spelling variation. Hindi has far more of it, and no normaliser can resolve it, because the variants are not a fixed mapping between two conventions. The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, a list of the spellings that are accepted as correct.

Monsoon is small measured in hours and large measured in speakers. That is the design, and it is where most of the value sits.

Speaker concentration and diversity beyond the fields above.

Three properties follow, and each is a claim about variance rather than volume.

No voice carries the score: The ten largest contributors account for between 2.8% and 6.8% of total duration, and more than half of all speakers appear exactly once. A result on Monsoon is an average over hundreds of distinct voices, not a small number of talkers recorded at length. Test sets of comparable duration are usually constructed the other way.

No region or handset carries it either: The Indian English public set draws on 428 native districts across 30 states and union territories; the Hindi sets, being a Hindi-belt language, concentrate more tightly but still span 202 and 295 districts. Recordings come from 315 to 582 distinct device models, with no single model exceeding 2.1% of segments in any subset. Corpora collected on standardised hardware overfit to one microphone response; this one cannot.

Indian English here is not one accent: This is English as it is spoken across the country, not the English of one region. All six zones are represented: in the public set, 35% of segments are contributed by southern speakers, 18% from the East, 18% from Central, 16% from the North and 11% from the West. The accent variation that follows from that spread is recorded in the metadata rather than asserted.

Monsoon ships 18 columns per segment, of which 12 are metadata, where most public ASR test sets ship an identifier, a transcript and a duration. Demographic fields are complete or near-complete; contributors consented to this use.

The two languages have different geographic shapes, and the shape is informative. The Hindi sets concentrate in the Hindi belt, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for roughly 40% of speakers, which is what a Hindi corpus sampled by population should look like. The Indian English sets are much flatter: no state exceeds 13%, and a third of speakers come from outside the eight largest. Public and private halves match closely on both.

Indian state boundaries were drawn along linguistic lines, so district and state carry real accent signal, which is why these fields are released rather than summarised away. Analysis of this kind has been reported at scale for Indian ASR: district-level error rates spanning roughly 4% to 44%, with underrepresented regions well behind the Hindi belt and the metros, plus disaggregation by audio quality, speaking rate, utterance duration, gender, age and device. Those runs were on a closed benchmark. Monsoon makes the same class of analysis possible on a public leaderboard test set.

Broad geographic coverage requires recruitment across hundreds of districts rather than longer sessions from fewer speakers, and distributed recruitment at this scale introduces failure modes that a smaller collection does not face: contributors gaming the task, played-back audio submitted as live speech, and inattentive annotation. Each is addressed by an explicit check.

Recruitment and recording: Contributors were recruited through the Voice Arena community, a global digital platform whose reach extends into the rural and semi-urban districts that speech corpora rarely cover. Pairs then recorded two-person conversations over a peer-to-peer interface, dual-channel, on assigned everyday topics. Contributors used their own handsets and their own connections. Many of those are low-end devices on unstable bandwidth, which is why that condition is present in the released audio rather than filtered out of it. Prospective contributors completed a language proficiency screening before being granted recording access, were compensated, and provided informed consent covering use in training and distribution. A per-speaker duration cap, calibrated per language to the population size and geographic distribution of its speakers, prevented a small number of prolific contributors from dominating a language or region; more than half of the speakers in these sets contribute exactly one segment.

Elicitation: Eliciting spontaneous speech at scale presents its own difficulty, as contributors tend to produce short and sparse responses without structured guidance. Each conversation was therefore seeded with an open-ended narrative cue and progressively revealed follow-up questions, spanning domains including travel, healthcare, agriculture, education and digital services, guiding the exchange toward extended description without scripting it. Candidate topics were generated with large language models, then reviewed and localised by native-speaker linguists.

Quality control: Every recording passed a set of gating checks prior to transcription. The spoken language was verified against the assigned language using language identification models trained on human-annotated data across more than 30 languages. Speaker gender was confirmed against the self-reported label using a dedicated classifier, applied as corroboration of the self-report rather than as a replacement for it. A further model distinguished genuine spontaneous conversation from pre-recorded or played-back audio. Signal-to-noise ratio estimation removed recordings degraded beyond intelligibility, while natural environmental background noise was deliberately preserved so that the acoustic realism of in-the-wild speech is retained. Recordings clearing these checks were segmented by voice activity detection, split at two seconds of continuous silence or at a fifteen-second soft cap closed at the next detected silence. Segmentation was applied independently per channel, so every segment is single-speaker and single-channel. Segments then passed a DNSMOS P.808 check.

Transcription: Reference transcripts are human work. A first draft was generated by internal ASR models trained on in-domain data, none of which appear on any public leaderboard, so no system evaluated on these sets contributed to the references it is scored against. Every subsequent stage was performed by native-speaking linguists under a five-level protocol built on a strict separation of labour, in which each correction round is followed by an independent verification round performed by a different annotator, so no linguist audits their own output. A linguist first corrects the draft segment by segment against the acoustic signal; a second re-verifies it and flags residual disagreements. Subsequent levels iterate this cycle with fresh annotators, progressively resolving ambiguous phonetic realisations, code-switching boundaries, named entities, and orthographic consistency across spelling variants. Numerals are written as words, so that the transcript corresponds directly to what was spoken. Segments still flagged at the final level were returned for re-transcription before admission. Annotator behaviour was monitored automatically throughout, flagging submissions containing characters outside the target script, unnatural character or word repetitions, and unusually low or high edit counts.

What follows is one example, run on the public Indian English split, to show the kind of evaluation the metadata makes possible. It is not the finding the sets exist to deliver; it is an illustration of what becomes answerable once every clip carries a speaker.

Eight models on the leaderboard land between 4.81 and 4.99 WER on this set. That is 0.18 points from best to worst, inside what five hours can resolve. Ranked on the corpus, they are the same model.

Grouping speakers by region tells a different story. Each speaker's native district is rolled up to its zonal council, the Ministry of Home Affairs grouping of Indian states, giving five well-sampled zones. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo varies by 0.46 points across them. mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507, fourteen hundredths of a point behind it on the corpus, varies by 1.68, running 4.38 in the Central zone against 6.06 in the East. Two systems that are indistinguishable on the leaderboard differ almost fourfold in how much their accuracy depends on where the speaker is from.

Which zone is hardest is not fixed either. ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b is worst in the North, microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR-HF in the South, mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 in the East. If a single region were simply harder to transcribe, every model would rank the zones the same way. They do not, which points at the models rather than the audio.

Region is one of twelve recorded attributes, and the zones above are a coarse rollup of 428 districts. The same breakdown runs on age, education, occupation and handset, and the released files carry everything needed to reproduce it. None of it is available for a test set that records only what was said.

English orthographic variation is bounded. British against American spelling, punctuation, casing, digits against words: a normaliser can map most of it to a single form, and the leaderboard's does. Hindi is not bounded in the same way. Everyday speech is heavily code-mixed, English-origin words have no settled Devanagari spelling, and compound forms are written joined or separated according to preference. A single phrase can have ten or more valid written forms, and no fixed mapping collapses them, because there is no canonical side to map to.

Scored with a single reference, WER rewards a system for producing the spelling the annotator happened to choose. Two systems that recognised the audio equally well can differ by several points on orthography alone.

The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, the set of written forms accepted as correct. Building it is manual work. Candidate variants are drawn from multiple ASR transcripts of the same audio and expanded with language models, then native-speaker linguists decide which are valid for that utterance and prune the rest, so only forms consistent with what was said are admitted.

Thus, for Hindi we report the Orthographically-Informed Word Error Rate (OIWER), introduced by AI4Bharat, instead of WER. A hypothesis is aligned against the accepted set at each span, so any admitted form counts as correct and only genuine recognition errors are charged.

To quantify the effect, the same hypotheses were scored twice. Flattening each lattice to its first variant per span yields a single string reference of the kind a conventional benchmark provides; any of the admitted variants would serve equally well, and a different choice would yield a different reference. Scored against the flattened reference, error rates rise for every system, and they do not rise uniformly. Rankings change as a consequence. The figure below shows two pairs of systems that reverse order between the two references: under a single reference a system is rewarded in part for reproducing the annotator's orthography, whereas the lattice scores only recognition.

We also open source our implementation, voi-oiwer, so every result on these sets can be reproduced directly.

For the private splits, get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard and the Hugging Face team will run the evaluation. As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:

Indian-English joins the main leaderboard as Voice Arena Monsoon, in the default column set rather than as an opt-in toggle, so it contributes to the headline Average WER for every model. The private split feeds the aggregated Private (conversational) column alongside Appen and DataoceanAI data. The public and private Hindi appears in the Multilingual tab, where a model is ranked only if it supports every selected language, making that column a like-for-like comparison. Alternative, select "Hindi" from the "Language dataset breakdown" dropdown menu.

Hindi is a sharp case of a general problem. Any language written more than one way, spoken by people a benchmark has not sampled, carries both of the failures described here. These sets do not fix them. What they add is a way to see them: a test set on a leaderboard the field already watches, carrying enough about each speaker and each reference that a difference between two systems can be traced to who was talking and how they write it, instead of disappearing into one number.

These four sets are part of Monsoon, Voice Arena's broader dataset initiative for the Global South.

#9930. 30 years of Internet transfers with curl

Thirty years ago, on November 11, 1996 the young Brazilian student Rafael Sagula posted the source code for his tiny HTTP download tool online. That was httpget 0.1: a little over 100 lines of C code. Bare bones source code with almost no error checks and limited functionality.

When I found the source code of that initial httpget release just days after Rafael put it online, I had no idea how HTTP worked. The language to speak over the network to ask for resources. Okay, I already knew we call it protocol but not a lot more. I also had never heard of neither httpget nor Rafael before. I imagine that I found httpget by searching on Altavista since this was before Google, but I can’t recall the details.

Seeing the simplicity of this code it was not difficult to immediately spot the fundamental basics of the protocol. I presume maybe in the same vain how countless others in decades to follow also have thought of it when seeing the details for the first time. Much later I would come to understand that to be an illusion of simplicity, but in those early days I was more amazed and fascinated. I already enjoyed doing network programming and HTTP reasoned with me at once.

httpget 0.1 was almost completely without error checks and it used plain IPv4 addresses; no hostnames or URLs.

I, still a naive and enthusiastic developer with an Open Source mindset (even though that term would not be established until 15-16 months later), addressed some immediate bugs I ran into and added name resolving to the tool. I made diffs and emailed patches over to Rafael; the standard way we exchanged code changes back then. I knew about RCS and CVS for version control, but the use of these tools was spotty. It would actually take until September 1999 until I adopted CVS fully for the curl project. We later switched to using git in 2010.

The average internet connection speed of a normal household in Sweden, where I lived and I still live, in 1996 was 30 kbps. 30 kilobit per second. This was before v90 came and bumped the modems up to 56 kilobits. Ordinary mortals connected to the internet using modems over their single phone lines. Today, the average Swedish connection speed is 200 megabits/second.

Thirty years ago there were just 36 million global Internet users and 250,000 websites. Compared to the 6 or 7 billion users and 1 billion websites of today.

We used simpler protocols and while encrypted protocols like SSL existed, they were not used a lot and only for a few rare sites.

In November 1996, my main home computer was still an Amiga 3000 powered by a 25Mhz 68030 CPU but in early 1997 I upgraded to a faster and more modern machine: an Intel Pentium 120Mhz. I ran Windows 95 on this thing, and its prime use was to run an X server so that I could connect to my work computers and pop up X11 terminals at home. I built the first versions of httpget remotely on SunOS, Solaris and Dell Unix – because they happened to be what we had running at work.

I installed and tested Linux for the first time at work in 1997. I got our first public web servers up and of course I made sure curl worked fine on it. I did not switch to Linux on my home machine until 2000 when I also updated to an Intel Pentium III 733 Mhz box.

In 1996 I was working as a software developer doing embedded systems and Unix development in C, for a small Swedish company called Frontec Railway Systems. While working there, I came to learn about and enjoy IRC, and in my spare time a few friends and I developed an IRC bot we called Dancer. Spare time developing a TCP client written in C.

As the IRC bot slowly grew more capable, I wanted to use its extension capability and provide a currency translation service for the participants in the channel (the IRC term for a chat room). In an international channel like ours, we frequently discussed the price of things and having the bot able to quickly explain how much a hundred German Marks equaled in US Dollars could be a useful service.

My currency service needed to update currency rates maybe once per day so that it could use decently accurate rates. I found an HTTP page listing a bunch of currency rates and the httpget tool for doing the downloads, and then the bot could offer up-to-date currency rate translations. All was good.

I discovered computers and programming as a teenager on a Commodore 64. I got hooked immediately. I first learned Basic and moved on to 6510 assembler pretty quickly. In the late 1980s me and my friends had demo groups where we would write cool demos (and some game attempts) in assembler (under the group name Horizon). I established my habit of spending spare time on programming back then.

In the early 1990s I moved over to Amiga, started writing a text editor, got my first job at IBM where I truly got into a lot of C and Unix for the first time. Together with some friends we ran a BBS (The Holy Grail), for which we eventually would write our own BBS software; me and my brother Björn. I learned Motorola 68000 assembler on the Amiga. I wrote 8086 assembler on PC.

I never attended university. I got my first computer job at IBM when I was twenty. I then thought I would take the uni route later, but I never did. I remain uneducated.

In the early 1990s I discovered both the Internet and the world of freely available source code and I was hooked.

Rafael was not terribly keen on dealing with my patches for httpget. I believe he mostly just put his code out without any particular desire to do anything more with it. Instead I became the httpget maintainer and kept polishing it. My main project was Dancer, the IRC bot. httpget was just a side-project to make sure the currency service kept working fine.

At some point I fell over a gopher site that provided many more currency rates than the HTTP page I was scraping at the time so of course I had to add support for that as well to the download tool. With gopher support added, it was not just http anymore and the name of the tool was no longer accurate. It became urlget. A third listing was found that provided rates over FTP and, yes, I added support for that protocol as well.

Already from the start I made the source code available under a free license, continuing what Rafel kicked off. He hosted the first releases, but during 1997 I took over and hosted the tarballs on the website I set up and administrated for work. I told my friends and the news about the tool slowly spread. I started getting bug reports from users and occasionally someone sent me patches to fix problems or add features.

This was a time of many Unix flavors and as I wanted widest possible use and adoption, I knew that I needed help and assistance from friends to make sure it built and ran fine on all those different systems.

In the beginning of 1998 I added upload support to the urlget tool (both FTP upload and HTTP POST) and again I realized the name of the tool was wrong. I decided I should try a name that contains the word URL, that can be pronounced in English and that is easy (and short) to type on a keyboard. cURL it was.

The leading ‘c’ could be short for client but I also liked that the name could be pronounced as see URL, as the tool would display the resource at the URL. You would see it (in a terminal). Naming things is hard.

curl 4.0 was released on March 20, 1998. By then it had grown to 3,300 lines of code and it featured 24 command line options and it spoke three protocols.

Gradually I lost interest in the IRC bot and the currency service but I stuck with curl. People used it, I got feedback, it improved.

I started and participated in several other Open Source projects, but curl remained my main baby and focus.

The concept of a function library that offers useful functionality to other programs is a concept I learned already on my Amiga days. As an example, I wrote the scripting language (FPL) for our Amiga text editor (FrexxEd) as a library, and we could later use that language for our BBS software, FrexxLink (which ran on OS/2) as well as in Dancer, the IRC bot.

A library is sort of next-level cool: not only is the source code available for everyone, but the functionality is as well; in an easy-to-use way.

The idea of converting curl into a library was already in the back of head from the start and in the summer of 2000 I refactored the internals and in August that year we introduced the first ever libcurl. Maybe someone else wants to do Internet transfers in their services or tools? Turns out some did!

One of the first adopters of libcurl was the PHP language which almost immediately decided that libcurl would become their default internet transfer engine. Being a key component and therefore part of their success journey helped getting users, getting testing, bug reports, feature requests and making the library solid.

curl is a child of the 1990s. Back then there were not a lot of options and language alternatives if you wanted to write a program that would easily build and run on most available operating systems and CPU architectures. Sure, C++ maybe could have been an option but I never liked it – and I still don’t. I’m also a strong believer in continuous and non-stop improvements and iterations; not rewrites. curl was never rewritten and if I get my way, it never will be. We do however repeatedly refactor and rearchitect internals to adapt to a changing world.

I wanted curl to be usable by everyone on every machine so it was designed and written for that purpose from the start. The source code in a portable way and the license in a liberal way.

We did most things wrong at the beginning but we learned, adapted, tried again, iterated and we kept doing release after release. Gradually we learned and did better. Every release with lots of bugs fixed and often a few new features. I kept spending my spare time on curl. Every day, every week, every year. Given enough time, something great can grow.

I did my first twenty-three years of this journey with curl only as my hobby. While curl happened, life also happened in parallel. I have switched jobs many times. I got married, bought a house, got two kids, and saw the kids grow up to be amazing adults. Somewhere in there I also managed to convert my hobby into my full time job. Living the dream.

curl is my life. My life is curl. I have been invited and able to speak to audiences hundreds of times in a dozen countries. I have received multiple awards and even gold medals straight from the hands of royalties for my open source work.

I don’t have an end goal with curl and I never did. I just want it to do internet transfers the best way possible: fast, securely, using the proper protocols in optimal ways. There is no rush towards anything. It is just a non-stop walk forward with never-ending polish and tightening every bolt there is.

Thirty years have flown by and yet the development pace is still intense. We regularly implement new transfer protocol features before anyone else. We have leading implementations for lots of network solutions. We ship code that carries a huge portion of the world’s internet infrastructure on its shoulders without fuss.

I still enjoy building things. Writing code to create something that did not exist before; and maybe even more so to make the program actually do things users want and like. I enjoy fixing bugs partly for that reason, but I also like the puzzle and the challenge of debugging and solving tricky problems. Designing a software architecture, coming up with APIs and figuring out how to provide powerful network transfer functionality to power billions of devices are things that make me eager to get started again every morning – still after thirty years.

It never really gets done. The world of the Internet and its transfers keeps changing. New protocols, new versions, new flavors, new third party libraries, new build tools and environments force us to constantly change and adapt.

I want curl to be a leader in internet transfers, its protocol implementations and every aspect of the project. I want us to be an exemplary Open Source project and run every tiny piece of it in an almost excessively transparent and progressive way. curl should be a top contender for the most-secure software component you can find. Our project should be friendly and welcoming to newcomers, both users and developers and not the least, there can be no other software project to compete with the amount, the accuracy and the plethora of documentation. Not to mention that we never break APIs or ABIs. Applications and scripts should be able to keep running, unmodified, even when they upgrade curl. Until the end of times.

I’m a firm believer in iterating and never rewriting. We fix, we refactor and we clean up but rewriting into another language or even using the same language is out of the question.

Simply put: software engineering done right.

While curl speaks more than two dozen protocols (at least counting URL schemes), it has always been most known for HTTP(S) and I think we put the most work and efforts into its HTTP engine. We know lots of people use curl for debugging HTTP in general and their server implementations in particular. We were early adopters of both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. We are often told people use our way of speaking HTTP and our source code as guidance for how things should be done. This is an honor and a huge responsibility that we take seriously.

After I first had learned about HTTP from reading httpget source code and then of course studied the RFC documentation explaining the specifics. In the late 2000s I learned about the HTTPbis effort and joined the mailing list for the HTTP specification update in the works. In 2009 I participated in my first ever IETF meeting that took place in Stockholm, Sweden. There, I got to meet some of the HTTP RFC authors and main people for the first time: Roy, Larry, Mark, Julian etc. They are all lovely people and I really felt that I would be able to make curl better by hanging out in the HTTP IETF circles more. I also wanted to contribute back my own experiences and viewpoints to maybe help improve the world ever so slightly.

That community later started the HTTP Workshop series out of which I have been to every single instance. Hanging out with the primary HTTP implementers in the world is fun, super educational and humbling. I believe this networking makes HTTP and all the involved  implementations even better.

curl is not a legal entity or a formal organization of any kind. It is a bunch of loosely connected people on the Internet who have a common goal, a few mailing lists, a website and some git repositories. curl is not hosted under any umbrella, not part of any larger organization and is not owned or controlled by any company. It is probably as free and independent as a software project can be. I believe this is an excellent position for curl and gives us maximum flexibility and control of our own destiny.

libcurl runs in an estimated thirty billion installations today. It is a rough estimate since the majority of all libcurl users never tell us they use it, but we need to find it mentioned in their credit screens, open source license windows or their manuals. A super popular app might use libcurl today and not tomorrow, or vice versa, which can make the numbers shift by several billions overnight. In reality of course, once the pulse raise has calmed down and your ego is content, these numbers do not matter. In our corner of the world, things don’t change notably when we go from a thousand installs to billions. We still work with similar people, in similar ways, with similar challenges.

For me, and for many others, the coolest place curl has been used is probably on Mars. It was confirmed by NASA that curl was used to aid the Mars landing mission, even if they don’t tell us exactly for what and where.

A ridiculously common question to me is “what is the weirdest place you’ve seen curl run?” I have ceased getting surprised about what devices and what things that are Internet connected and thus where curl runs. Light-bulbs, dish washers, AC units, heat pumps, cars, printers, blenders, ovens, toy robots, drones, guns, motorcycles, medical devices, fridges, soundbars and espresso machines. Of course in addition to all those “traditional” things we already expect to run curl: games, servers, cars, printers, TVs, watches, tablets, game consoles, blue-tooth speakers, routers, mobile phone apps and their operating systems.

Our modern society is keen at eventually making everything network connected, and once they are, they can use curl and libcurl to perform their transfers.

Benevolent Dictator For Life. A term popularly used to describe the steering mechanism of many Open Source projects. Basically a single person being the captain of the ship. The one who can commandeer the direction, who can dictate truths about the project and who says yes and no firmly. For better and for worse, I remain the BDFL for curl. I try to repeat that curl is not a solo-show and it was never a one-man circus. We are literally thousands of people who have contributed code, and every year there are hundreds of new authors helping out. I may remain the captain of the ship, but no ship above a certain size can be managed without a lot of additional man power and curl is no different.

I may very well remain BDFL for a long time to come because I love my role and because I don’t know any other way to live my life or to run the curl project. There are no succession plans and I am against doing such. There is no heir or vice-BDFL prepared to take over. Instead we document everything and every detail so there are no secrets, so that no formal hand-over should be necessary (except for some rare passwords). If I get run over by a truck tomorrow, you guys can figure it out and continue. You don’t need me.

My email address is commonly listed in the regular curl license and this license is usually included in license listings, credit screens or manuals. When random people run into problems or issues with products in this modern society, they often struggle to find someone to help them. There is no one to contact or ask. My email then sometimes serves as a last resort to finally get the answers they’ve been fighting for. I frequently get emails about products I never knew existed, I certainly didn’t know they used curl and I for sure don’t know how to help the users with their problems…

The much darker side of the traces curl usage leaves in products, is when malicious tools, services and attackers use tools that can be associated with me and my email address. I have been accused of various attacks and “hacking” people and companies multiple times. I have received death threats multiple times and I strongly suspect that my US visa problems were triggered by something in these veins.

I stick to the Open Source ethos and spirit. It is a fundamental part of my belief system and I am convinced this is the superior way to produce software to build society on. I do everything I can to stick to the liberal license curl is shipped under because I love the concept. It is however not an easy pitch: give everything away for free and then try to get someone to pay for it. I think it is fair to say that if I wanted to optimize for money, I should have played this one out differently. That would have been another life. Not my life.

Of course I feel immensely proud of what we have accomplished. The little toy thing in 1996 kicked off a journey that led to the creation and continued maintenance of a modern Internet infrastructure cornerstone. We have reached this point, not by talking, not by using marketing nor by tricking someone into using our code. We conquered the world by shipping consistent top quality over several decades. curl runs in all these devices and services done by all those companies because it is the right choice for them, selected because it is Open Source, rock-solid and fast – and also likely to be around in the future. Everyone can depend on us to keep shipping updates in a proven stellar fashion and minimal friction. Forever and ever.

There are many dimensions of the future to consider here. The future of Open Source. The future of curl. The future of internet transfers. The future of the C programming language and the future for me, personally. At least.

I don’t think I can guess the future any better than other humans. I was never good at it and I never really tried to. I always only focus on the next coming months and make quick adjustments when things make turns.

I think Open Source is a solid way to do foundational software, now and in the future. It will continue to have a funding problem and too many projects live and die with a single maintainer. But building common and open building blocks is simply a requirement for speedy development, for building reliable components and for being able to produce products and services at the speed we seem to want. I don’t believe AI will kill Open Source.

I think curl has many more years of service ahead. Primarily because it is the trusted solution and nothing else is even close to this long proven track record, secondarily because it runs on all platforms like no alternatives. I do not rule out that it will be replaced by an alternative at some point, when projects written in C are gradually phased out. (If they ever are.)

Internet transfers in general seem like a fundamental idea that probably is going to be around in a similar style for a long time. The protocols will keep evolving, changing and getting updated but the client/server/protocol concept seems solid and likely to be here for the long term.

I personally will keep working on curl and Internet transfers for as long as I think it is fun and challenging. I turn 56 years old in a few weeks. I hope to be able to spend several more decades on this.

Thank you mom and dad for your understanding and supporting attitude when I as a teenager got completely sucked into a world of computers and programming. Thanks Björn and Kjell for all the awesome times and all the fun when we learned development together and took our first stumbling steps as programmers. Thanks to the Horizon team for the fun and all the demos, copy parties we did and attended. Thanks to Huddinge Vi Unga who owned the machine and sponsored the dual phone connections for our BBS for several years as we discovered fidonet and a world of people and communication. Thanks Jonas for getting me that first job at IBM when I had no work experience at all. Thanks to Bjørn for co-creating the Dancer bot project with me to the people in #amiga IRC chat on Efnet and then IRCnet for your support. Thanks to my bosses at Frontec in the mid 1990s who allowed me to do spare time development on their various Unix machines (even though you probably were not aware of the full extent). Thanks to all the early users and adopters of curl who pushed me forward and who brought it into all the important Linux distros early on and showed me this thing had legs. Thanks Anja, my wife, for keeping up with me spending all this time in front of my machines, and for sometimes boring you to death rambling about some miniscule detail from the curl project that I couldn’t let go from my mind. Thanks to my kids Agnes and Rex for being the lights of my life, for being awesome and for not being particularly impressed by or interested in what I do. You do your life. Thanks to everyone who ever contributed to the curl project, in whatever capacity. In particular, thanks to Stefan, Viktor, James, Viktor, Dan, Jay, Daniel, Max for being part of the core maintainer team for ages. Thanks to Björn, Kjell and Linus of Haxx for being awesome friends and always supporting me and curl whenever it has been needed – and for the Rockbox side-adventure of course. Thanks to Larry at wolfSSL for believing in me and curl enough to allow me to work on curl full-time without even blinking. Thanks to all curl sponsors, donors and to all awesome paying customers of curl support, who combined are what makes it possible for me to do what I do. Thanks to everyone who ever invited me to conferences and events to talk and meet people. Thanks to Patrik who nominated me to the Polhem Prize award that I then received in the form of a gold medal. Thanks Michael for nominating me for the IVA gold medal. Thanks to all others whose names I forgot to include here.

Thanks to everyone who uses curl and continues to participate in curl development.

Yes. We have two separate birthdays: httpget was born in November 1996. curl was born in March 1998.

Rafael Sagula unfortunately left us much too early. He died in 2016. I am grateful for him kick-starting this thing for us.

Irc ! Those were the days. Netscape Navigator and dial-up. What fun. I used Dans mIRC. Oh joy!

#9929. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks, but it doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.
