#9897. Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Organizations may not be ready for completely autonomous communication processes, but there are places where automating information updates would alleviate pressure.

Organizations steadily deploy automated threat detection and response processes; some even take it a step further with fully artificial intelligence (AI) security operations centers (SOCs). Automation can catch an incident in seconds, yet communication remains mostly manual across an industry that requires more transparency.

The disconnect can strain relationships and trust as customers wait for incident impact and mitigation answers. Hands-on communications also put more pressure on chief information security officers (CISOs), who must relay timely updates to IT personnel and executives as the incident clock winds down.

Incident response (IR) communications are increasingly too much for humans to coordinate without more help. But disclosures contain sensitive information — the status of a company's security posture or how they responded when alerted to an incident — and automation takes away some of the control leadership wants to hold onto in regard to timing and specifics.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

From a coordination and information standpoint, automating communications is absolutely important, says Tim Brown, chief strategy officer at Cytactic. That could mean implementing a centralized place to view everyone's status versus relying on meetings to receive updates.

A dedicated crisis communication platform could help, Brown says. A single click of a button could notify everyone, and that includes contingency options if normal communications go down, which is typical following an incident where systems go offline.

Brown is no stranger to hectic IR communication scenarios. While trying to manage the SolarWinds attack fallout, the former CISO got pulled into one crisis after the other. He oversaw five different teams, coordinated tasks, scheduled meetings, received updates from everyone, and tried to keep the customers briefed.

As he looks back now, he appreciates how much help everyone around him was. Still, some preparation was missing: more tabletop exercises, meeting the appropriate people beforehand, and technology to ease communications.

IR communications are complicated. Organizations may wait to disclose certain information, so they do not tip off attackers. Sometimes victim organizations post customer-only private advisories, but that leaves public awareness and downstream victims vulnerable. Yet other times, companies simply choose not to disclose or downplay effects to save face.

The Securities and Exchange Commission and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) continue to update and adopt new disclosure regulations in light of more disruptive attacks. The Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) of 2022, after missing several earlier deadlines, is nearing finalization. Once in effect, the rule would require covered entities to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours of discovery, and critical infrastructure organizations that make ransom payments would need to report within 24 hours.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Even if organizations want to disclose any information in good faith, that poses challenges. A wide net of victims, third parties, and supply chain risks abound. It's increasingly more difficult to even know who is affected these days.

Douglas McKee, director of vulnerability intelligence at Rapid7, ventures to guess that most security leaders would cite communication problems, and they usually exist long before an incident ever happens. For example, security teams tend to talk in terms of common vulnerability exposures (CVEs) and indicators of compromise, while the people making business decisions need to know what any of that actually means.

On a normal day, that gap is annoying, but during an incident, the language barrier gets amplified because everyone needs answers at the same moment, even though the facts change by the hour. And nobody wants to be the person who said the wrong thing publicly, McKee adds.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"Third parties make this even harder," he tells Dark Reading. "I've seen plenty of situations where a vendor knows about a problem in their product well before their customers do, but the notification lands in a generic inbox or goes to a contact who left the company two years ago.”

Attackers benefit from that confusion, he notes, adding how important it is for defenders to agree internally on what's happening so they can relay information to customers confidently.

Organizations want to be more transparent but continually struggle with how to personalize communication outreach, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Whether in day-to-day fraud communications or during an active incident, the more they can leverage AI, insights, and understanding the better they can adapt, he adds .

Right now, it's easier to automate detection and response because the inputs can be fairly structured, explains McKee; a log entry either matches a rule or it doesn't. IR communication, on the other hand, involves judgement calls with legal and reputational consequences.

"Organizations are understandably nervous about letting a machine decide what goes out the door with their name on it," McKee says. "Let's face it: An analyst can shrug off a false positive in a few minutes, but there's no easy way to 'unsend' an inaccurate breach notice to your customers."

That doesn't mean automating communication is off the table — it just needs to be pointed at the right parts of the problem, he says. Organizations can automate pulling together the incident timeline or tracking which stakeholders have been notified and when. McKee also recommends using tools to draft a first version of an update from data the responders already have.

It's all about freeing people up to spend their time on decisions that actually need a human. The way McKee looks at it, "automation should get the draft in front of the right person faster, and that person should still be the one who verifies and hits send."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9896. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9895. Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Android device manufacturer Videostrong allegedly ran the operation, which infected set-top boxes and IoT devices with a backdoor to create infrastructure for criminal activity.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, a cybercriminal operation that planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android-based set-top boxes, turning consumer devices into infrastructure for malicious activity.

The operation, attributed with "high confidence" by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to Android device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co., involved deliberately embedding the XCPE backdoor malware in multiple device models and brands since at least 2024, according to a blog post published earlier this week by GTIG.

Rather than simply exploiting vulnerable devices, however, the manufacturer allegedly built a system that allowed criminal affiliates to access compromised hardware and deploy their own malicious software, Google said.

"Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices," according to the post. "These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices."

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Google and its partners, which included Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, took legal action against Videostrong to disrupt the domains and servers it used to control the botnet, install affiliate malware modules, and operate the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by those modules.

Because the affiliate modules "each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE," Google assessed that disrupting their C2 infrastructure "will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to the post.

Google has also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the manufacturer, along with any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. Videostrong did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment on Wednesday.

Most devices infected by the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes. However, the botnet also included other Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage systems, according to Google.

This wider exposure of IoT devices is reflected in Bitdefender's "2026 IoT Security Landscape Report," released this week. The findings recorded 5.4 billion security events and 6.2 billion vulnerability observations across devices behind approximately 10.4 million monitored routers between January and September 2026. While these figures represent detected activity and identified device vulnerabilities rather than confirmed compromises, they underline the scale of the threat facing connected devices and the potential attack surface they present to businesses.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

While most of Videostrong's interactions with victim devices involved installing, uninstalling, and configuring malware modules, operators also carried out so-called "sensitive actions," according to Google. These include capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive information, such as account and device details, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including those used to establish reverse shells on infected devices.

Although the operation primarily targeted consumer devices, it has significant security implications for businesses and enterprise organizations. XCPE demonstrates how compromised IoT equipment can be turned into criminal infrastructure, providing attackers with residential proxy networks that help conceal malicious activity, evade IP-based security controls, and facilitate fraud.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"By turning 1.3 million devices into residential proxies, threat actors fuel the exact infrastructure used to attack high-value API endpoints," says Mark Mazur, field chief technology officer (CTO) for mobile application security firm Approov.

Because attacks launched through the botnet can originate from legitimate consumer IP addresses, standard security defenses such as geo-blocking, ASN blocking, and IP reputation filters "are practically useless against them," he says.

"They are creating infrastructure, largely based on IoT devices, that can power sophisticated credential stuffing and API abuse campaigns," Mazur adds.

The malware's ability to execute remote commands, conduct network reconnaissance, and maintain persistent access also raises concerns about connected devices deployed in corporate and healthcare environments. Digital signage, televisions, and telehealth equipment, for example, could provide attackers with an opportunity to explore networks or establish a foothold if compromised devices are connected to inadequately segmented networks. Google has not confirmed that any such activity has occurred, however.

Google requires original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to undergo a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to participate in the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong was able to evade these checks by "employing obfuscation techniques" that exploited a weakness in the review process, according to Google. The malicious code was loaded after the device's first boot, allowing it to bypass the initial security checks.

Calling Videostrong's actions "an unacceptable breach of trust," Google said it has since strengthened its review processes to protect the integrity of Android TV firmware and "better safeguard against similar activity in the future," according to the post.

As an additional protective measure, Google encouraged consumers to be wary of applications offering payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your Internet," as these could turn their set-top boxes and other IoT products into part of a residential proxy network.

"These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device's home network," according to the post.

Google also urged Android users to stick to trusted app stores, review the permissions requested by third-party VPN and proxy applications, and ensure built-in security protections such as Google Play Protect are active.

Finally, Google called on mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces, and other technology providers to continue sharing threat intelligence and implementing security best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software to prevent similar botnet operations from emerging in the future.

InfoQ Homepage News Angular's TypeScript 7-Powered Compiler Enters Beta with Rust-Based Preprocessor

Nov 11, 2026 2 min read

The Angular team has shared details of a new version of its compiler, the Angular Preprocessor (ngp), which rewrites the analysis stage of the toolchain in Rust to clear the way for TypeScript 7 adoption. Alex Rickabaugh and Mark Techson announced the work on the Angular team blog in late September, shortly after Microsoft shipped TypeScript 7.0, whose Go-based rewrite removed the ts.Transformer API that Angular's ahead-of-time compiler depends on.

The existing compiler, ngc, wraps tsc and uses the Transformer API to turn decorators such as @Component and @Pipe into runtime instructions. The Go port offers no cross-language equivalent, and crossing the JS/Go boundary at every file would be prohibitive. The Angular team's answer is to decouple compilation from TypeScript's APIs and rebuild it on Oxc, the VoidZero Rust toolchain already powering Vite. The team pointed to the plan on X, framing it as a partial rewrite rather than a fresh start.

ngp runs in three stages. A Rust frontend using Oxc analyses files in parallel to discover Angular declarations and resolve metadata. The existing TypeScript template compiler then emits two artefacts, a runtime file containing the transformed component and a .ngtypecheck.ts file holding the Type Check Block (TCB) for template type-checking. Finally a downstream tool, whether tsgo, tsrs, esbuild or Rolldown, handles type-checking and JavaScript emission independently.

The bulk of ngp landed on 8 October in a single commit of more than 370,000 lines, around 56,000 of them Rust. Cédric Exbrayat of Ninja Squad benchmarked the beta against three projects ranging from 15 to 1,714 components and measured a 2x to 3x speedup on cold builds, with memory use on the largest project falling from 2.8 GB to 1.4 GB. Pairing ngp with tsrs and Rolldown gave the fastest pipeline, with tsgo and esbuild only marginally slower. They concluded there is further gains to be made:

This is already very promising, and there are certainly further gains to be made when the team focuses on performance optimization.

Christopher Holder at push-based.io took a different tack, writing vite-plugin-ngp to compile Angular files on demand. On the Super Productivity codebase (252 components), the dev server reached the first page in 10.5 seconds against 17.4 for ng serve, with template edits applying in 112 milliseconds rather than a 2.6 second full reload. On a generated 5,000-component app the gap widened to 1.6 seconds against 28.4. Holder cautioned that the plugin "is a prototype on a prototype" pinned to 22.3.0-next.2.

On Reddit, a number of developers are excited about the update and write up, with one commenting:

Read the whole article. Impressive. The Angular team surpassed my expectations!

VoidZero's own experimental Oxc Angular compiler, covered by InfoQ in April, reported a roughly 97% improvement on narrower workloads but is now described as "actively seeking maintainers". The Angular team confirmed VoidZero's work influenced the architecture and that the two groups have been collaborating, with ngp becoming the official path.

Teams on earlier Angular versions should first run the standard update guide to reach v20 or later. Adoption of ngp is expected to land in a minor release of Angular 22 once TypeScript 7.1 restores the compiler API; until then production builds should stay on ngc.

Angular is Google's open-source, TypeScript-first web framework, widely adopted across enterprise applications and built around standalone components and signal-based reactivity.

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. #9890. Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

An attacker could write arbitrary files and read sensitive files via images uploaded to the Rails Active Storage ImageMagick integration, possibly positioning a threat actor for lateral movement.

A critical vulnerability in Rails could send impacted Web servers off the tracks.

Rails, or Ruby on Rails, is a Web application framework built on Ruby. The framework's Active Storage component handles file uploads and can use the ImageMagick image processing suite to analyze uploaded images. Unfortunately, a flaw enables attackers to write arbitrary files to a Web server via ImageMagick.

The vulnerability (which is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9) is critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and is considered so severe because an attacker could upload a crafted image file to write arbitrary files, read sensitive files, and access secrets such as secret_key_base files, external system credentials, database passwords, and third-party tokens. These secrets could then be used for lateral movement or remote code execution into external systems.

As a GitHub advisory published by the Rails maintainers explains, "A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

The vulnerability exists because ImageMagick doesn't necessarily decide how to process a file (i.e., which coder it uses) based on the filename or extension, but rather on its contents. This means an attacker can upload an image file named "maliciousfile.jpeg" that contains content that causes ImageMagick to invoke a different coder. This can potentially allow arbitrary file reads or writes on the server.

Vulnerable versions of Active Storage include those 8.0 versions prior to 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 versions prior to 8.1.4.1. Those affected organizations running Rails applications that use ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing run with a security policy that does not block the affected coders, and accept uploads from untrusted users.

Active Storage patches are available now. The GitHub page includes further mitigation requirements for applications that use MiniMagick and ImageMagick.

Additionally, if an application stores attachments through the Disk service, users should "change secret_key_base and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens," the GitHub advisory said. Users should not retain exposed secrets as a fallback.

If a user requires a workaround, the GitHub page offers system rules the user can apply into ImageMagick's system policy.

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for exposure management vendor watchTowr, tells Dark Reading the firm has already reproduced the vulnerability in a lab environment, and "that against the right target, exploitation won't be difficult at all."

Moreover, he says he'd be surprised if public proof-of-concept exploit code took more than a few days to come to light.

"For attackers, reproducing the vulnerability here is likely the easy part, as the patterns and primitives involved in exploitation are well established," Knott says. "The hard part is finding software and deployments that are common enough, and configured in a vulnerable way, to deliver impact at scale indiscriminately."

#9889. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9886. SecurityDataPipeline.com Launches as a New Educational Resource for the AI Era

The ungated resource explains how security data pipelines reduce SIEM ingestion costs, preserve detection coverage, and prepare the data layer for AI-driven security operations.

BOSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Realm Security today launched SecurityDataPipeline.com, a new educational resource designed to help cybersecurity professionals understand security data pipelines and reduce SIEM costs without weakening detection coverage.

For many security teams, rising data volumes present a difficult choice between cutting data and keeping detections. Security data pipelines offer a way to address this challenge. Because they sit between security data sources and destinations, these platforms collect, process, filter, and route telemetry before it reaches a SIEM, data lake, or other security tool.

"Most security teams are being asked to cut SIEM spend and roll out AI agents at the same time, and both of those decisions come down to the data layer," said Chris O'Brien, VP of Marketing at Realm Security. "We built SecurityDataPipeline.com so practitioners can understand how pipelines work and how to reduce volume without losing detections, before they ever talk to a vendor, including us."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Security data pipelines are becoming essential infrastructure as AI reshapes the SOC. As enterprises deploy AI agents for triage, investigation, and response, the data layer underneath those agents determines whether those agents get clean, normalized context to reason over. SecurityDataPipeline.com is a resource for security leaders trying to understand how to turn raw logs and fragmented cybersecurity data into clean, actionable intelligence for AI SOC agents and other AI cybersecurity initiatives.

The resource also covers how security data pipelines route telemetry to destinations including Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, and Databricks Delta Lake; how OCSF-normalized data supports AI SOC agents; and how MITRE ATT&CK coverage can be preserved as teams reduce SIEM ingestion volumes.

On SecurityDataPipeline.com, visitors can:

Explore a beginner's guide explaining security data pipelines and their core functions.

Try an ungated interactive pipeline demonstration showing how security events are filtered, transformed, enriched, and routed.

Use a SIEM cost calculator estimating potential reductions in data ingestion costs.

Learn about practical use cases covering SIEM cost reduction, SIEM migration, SOC efficiency, data governance, and AI readiness.

Read technology comparisons explaining the differences between security data pipelines, SIEMs, data lakes, log forwarders, and observability pipelines.

The resource addresses how to reduce the cost of managing security data without weakening detection capabilities by looking at the role of data filtering, normalization, enrichment, routing, and retention. It also shows how teams can identify which information their security detections need and which data can be stored more economically.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

The website is intended for CISOs, security architects, SOC managers, and cybersecurity professionals evaluating ways to manage growing telemetry volumes.

SecurityDataPipeline.com is available at https://securitydatapipeline.com/.

Realm Security gives security teams independent control over their telemetry before it reaches the SIEM, data lake, or AI agent. The platform understands what each source produces and what each downstream system needs, then guides teams on what to keep, archive, and route. Headquartered in Boston, Realm deploys in about a week and typically cuts SIEM ingestion costs by 50% or more. Learn more at www.realm.security.

#9885. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9884. APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

After compromising websites, the Russian state-sponsored threat group is fingerprinting victims, then harvesting information from the interesting ones.

It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.

The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.

Researchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible.

"Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation."

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions.

Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.

In its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.

The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Each chain targeted specific vulnerabilities in iOS or Android that had remained unpatched on the exposed devices.

Related:Video Call Exploit Chains Two Flaws in Unisoc Modems

Sekoia said it found several indicators linking the campaign to APT29, including remnants of a separate 2025 watering-hole operation that researchers have previously attributed to the group. Sekoia also found signs that the attackers may have obtained their exploits from a third party, possibly a commercial surveillance vendor (CSV). The campaign's victims include organizations in Europe and the US, though most are based in Ukraine, a country that Russian threat groups have incessantly targeted since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

APT29's latest campaign is another indication of how mobile devices have become attractive intelligence targets for threat groups. Commercial spyware vendors are fueling the trend by making technology available that enables large scale surveillance and data theft via mobile devices. APT29's likely sourcing of the DarkSword exploit kit from a third-party provider suggests that sophisticated mobile intrusion capabilities that were once largely associated with highly targeted espionage operations are finding their way into broader campaigns.

"The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation," Sekoia warned. "Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9883. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9881. How do you actually self-host securely?

I recognize that the title is rather vague, but I'm completely green when it comes to self-hosting, so I figured here would be a good place to ask for some pointers given the discussions I sometimes see happening in the comments. I tried researching first through DDG and Google, but (and I recognize this might be a skill issue) most things I found are either SEO slop or trying to sell/market some service.

For some more context and to give a concrete example as to what I'm interested in, I got my hands on a Raspberry Pi which I'd like to use to start tinkering with self-hosting. My main goal would be to host my (static) website on it, potentially adding more things in the future.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting, so I'm curious whether it's viable to do it using open source tooling, any gotchas one might encounter, and generally any thoughts you might have on the topic.

(Also, feel free to suggest a tag other than devops, I figured security doesn't quite apply since it's a question and not a write-up/resource regarding security.)

It's safer to start with services that aren't public facing, e.g. install Tailscale on your phone, laptop, and Raspberry Pi, and then start setting up services you want for yourself.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting

I like to do the end-to-end myself but sometimes I just can't be bothered and so use Cloudflare Tunnels to make it work, and that's a better outcome for me than giving up entirely.

I've heard about Tailscale many times but, to be honest, their website reads the same as corporate emails to me, as in I cannot digest any substance from it (might be another skill issue, I know). Would you mind sharing some concrete use case for it (e.g. an example of what you use it for)? That might make it easier for me to grasp the concept.

The simplest way to explain it I think would be to say that Tailscale makes all your devices act like they’re on the same home network, no matter where they actually are.

Their site from 2020 is a bit clearer: https://web.archive.org/web/20201129111934/https://tailscale.com/

But basically it lets your various devices connect to each other, whereever they are, without having to deal with port forwarding, firewalls, dynamic DNS... so your phone or laptop can access self-hosted services on your Raspberry Pi (photos, Jellyfin, RSS, files, ...). It does this while keeping it all hidden from random people/attackers.

I don't use Tailscale, and instead just use plain Wireguard/mTLS, but Tailscale is easiest to set up and seems to be the most popular option for people that want to access their Raspberry Pi when away from home.

Specific example: say you want to have a job server whose dashboard you can access via a stable identifier, runs on an isolated machine, and is not exposed to the public internet. Then Tailscale is a great solution. Other examples: tunnels into other VPCs which should not be exposed to the internet; sharing local demos between those in the network; using a specific machine as an exit node when you don’t trust the network you’re currently on; access your devices via stable IDs (eg I have a cluster of Macs whose IPs are dynamic, but I can log in via screen share with stable IDs)

It sounds like what you may want is "nobody can read my packets but me!" If that's the case I would look at the chain of things.

These three are super intertwined, "self hosting" is choosing which of these you want to own.

You may end up using nginx or haproxy somewhere to get ports to line up. But you can also use iptables. Dealer's choice.

Tailscale and Cloudflare tunnels are really cool. They take a bit of the headache away, but you're right that they give up that bit of security (and the learning!).

I'm so psyched for you :) let me know how it goes!

I avoid exposing my services to the public internet since I am the only user. They are available only via WireGuard. I use plan WireGuard, but solutions like Tailscale or NetBird are fine if you need something else to deal with configuration for you.

On top of that, I still do HTTPs everywhere (using the ACME DNS-01 challenge so I get proper certificates from Let's Encrypt without exposing anything on the public Internet).

Authentication is mostly based on passkeys (I use PocketID for single-sing-on) and I only use SSH keys (backed by secure enclaves whenever possible).

I run my services in NixOS. For my threat model it's okay to run everything on the same machine but to get more workload segregation you could separate the various services across several VMs/micro-VMs.

How much you need to care about security is entirely dependent on what you host. I would for example greatly invested in security if I self-hosted a public facing file storage or an email server.

I would in general care much less if as you describe I would be hosting a static website on a Raspberry Pi. The risk just isn't that big. It can't cost you a lot of money since it's your own hardware. The worst thing that could happen is that a stranger gains complete control over your Raspberry Pi. They could possibly probe your local network (but not if you put the Rasberry Pi on a subnet), display other information on your website or put your Rasberry Pi to work on something benefitting them (as part of a botnet or crypto mining for example).

I personally wouldn't consider any of those possibilities as great risks. And as a bonus, setting up logging to detect if any of these were happening could be a fun side project.

instead of a cloudflare tunnel you could grab a vps, and tunnel with NAT. I do this for my torrent and DirectConnect clients, so they get public IPs without UPnP/NAT-PMP. I am considering doing same for Jellyfin so it's available outside of tailscale. But I might still require some extra layer, not sure.

I assume your internet connection has enough bandwidth to sustain a small to moderate website. Self-hosting a publicly facing service is an order of magnitude more dangerous than self-hosting private services such as photo management applications or media servers because of the security implications. On the bright side, static pages can be hosted securely with relatively low effort compared to LAMP stack.

(a) Applying network segmentation is a good start. The RPi should not be able to communicate with other devices through router / firewall configuration. Maybe allow just one device based on IP or MAC address to access the RPi from the LAN.

(b) Then setup DNS records. I assume you own an FQDN. Use an ready-made or custom script to update the DNS records. I'm using dnscontrol alongside envsubst and to perform the changes but there are simpler solutions out there.

(c) Once the DNS is working and updating properly, use an application to issue SSL certificates. My favourite is acme.sh but there are quite a few polished alternatives, e.g. certbot, lego, etc.

(d) Now you're ready to setup a reverse proxy. Note that modern rev-proxies like Caddy can manage (c) on their own. I'm not using them, I'm familiar with nginx so I use that.

(e) Create a deployment user with minimum permissions and use that user to upload data via sftp or other secure protocol. If you want to setup a deployment pipeline via git, that's also possible through webhooks.

(f) Secure the system. I'm pretty sure that you can flat-out ban the big cloud CIDRs. That will save you from dumb scanners abusing your website. Since very few humans use these addresses for outgoing connections, I think it's a good strategy to block them straight-up. You can setup a cron script to download CIDRs and update your firewall "block" tables.

f.1 Make sure you setup some sort of monitoring, so that you can quickly measure things like resources and even incoming requests (e.g. response latency, No of incoming requests, etc). Since you're going to self-host you'll have log access which means full visitors info.

f.2 You might want to explore the possibility of setting a "chroot"

f.3 Alerting: pushover is a good "host -> mobile" alternative, another is to setup the SMTPd in a way that the system can send you emails with status reports, etc. to your personal email.

(g) Backup everything locally (e.g. another NAS) or remotely (backblaze is fairly cheap), or both.

#9880. [$] Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers

Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.
