#9801. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9798. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

To run the model, upgrade the transformers package

Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results:

You can find more about this release in the Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH).

#9797. How AI Is Making Creativity More Homogeneous

AI CTO and systems builder. CTO of Archdesk; founder of Lextron.ai, Inclify and Rejsomat. I write on enterprise AI, agents and Joule Wars.

AI CTO and systems builder. CTO of Archdesk; founder of Lextron.ai, Inclify and Rejsomat. I write on enterprise AI, agents and Joule Wars.

AI CTO and systems builder. CTO of Archdesk; founder of Lextron.ai, Inclify and Rejsomat. I write on enterprise AI, agents and Joule Wars.

Here's an experiment you can describe in one line. Ask 25 language models for a metaphor about time, 50 times each, with the randomness turned up. You'd expect 1,250 attempts to cover some ground. They cover two ideas: time is a river, time is a weaver.

I went looking for results like that one because of something smaller. This autumn, friend after friend showed me the apartment they're about to build. Different cities, different budgets, different lives. The same room. Pale oak slats on one wall. A boucle sofa the colour of oat milk. An arch where a door used to be, linen curtains, one olive tree in a pot, a pendant lamp like a paper moon. By the third render I stopped looking at the picture and asked to see the prompt. Each of them had asked ChatGPT to show them their future home. It showed all of them the same one.

None of them knew. How would they? Each had seen exactly one render, their own, and it looked like taste. I was the only person in the story who had seen the set. From the inside, a default feels like a decision.

I build with these systems every day and I'm not going to stop. What follows is what I found when I went from the feeling to the measurements: what the models do alone, why the popular explanation is wrong, what happens when people use them, and where the money goes.

The full study threw 26,000 open-ended prompts at more than seventy models. A single model mostly repeated itself, and different models mostly repeated each other: cross-model similarity ran from 71 to 82 percent, and a typical cluster of fifty look-alike answers held the work of about eight different models. You can change your vendor. You'll get the same river.

None of this is new, only better measured. In January 2023 two researchers in Germany asked ChatGPT for a joke 1,008 times. More than 90 percent of what came back was the same 25 jokes, and one of them, about a scarecrow who won an award for being outstanding in his field, turned up 140 times. (Go and ask the chatbot in your other tab for a joke. I'll wait. If a scarecrow, a tomato or an atom is involved, you've just replicated a paper.)

The obvious reply is that people are no better. Ask a hundred humans about time and you'll hear about plenty of rivers. So a second team ran the comparison. Twenty-two models and 102 people took the same standard creativity tests. On the alternate-uses task, the one where you list things to do with an everyday object, the average distance between two humans' answers was 0.738. Between two models' answers it was 0.459. That gap is about two standard deviations, and a system prompt begging the models to "be very creative" closed less than half of it.

The detail I can't shake is that the models scored slightly higher than the people on individual originality. Any one answer was good, often better than yours or mine would have been. It was the set that was a monoculture.

You'd think there'd be a dial for this. Turn the temperature up, ask for something weird. But the Hivemind runs were already sampled hot. "Be very creative" bought back less than half the gap. A third team, comparing model-written book reviews with human ones, tried both tricks and barely moved their numbers. Temperature adds noise around the favourite answer. It doesn't change which answer is the favourite. To see why, you have to look at how these systems are finished, which is a different matter from how they're sampled.

The picture everyone reaches for, and the one I used myself, is the bell curve. The model learns the distribution of human work and hands you its middle. Everyone uses the same curve, so everyone gets the same middle. It's tidy, it's wrong, and the way it's wrong is the whole story.

Try it on my friends' living room. If you really averaged every living room on the internet you'd get a brown smear. The mean of a red sofa and a blue sofa is mud, and the mean of a thousand floor plans is fog. What ChatGPT drew was nothing like that. It was crisp and specific, a room you could order from a catalogue by Friday. An average is a blur of everything, and this was one particular thing. It wasn't averaged. It was picked.

The picking happens late. Pre-training teaches a model the whole messy distribution of what people have made, every cluster, with the empty space between them. Then comes post-training, the stage where people rate outputs and the model is tuned toward the ratings. That stage is an election, and it's held under a brutal rule. A 2025 paper from Meta's FAIR lab wrote the rule down: for the standard preference objective, putting all of the probability on the single highest-rated answer is an optimal solution. Winner takes all. And when two answers tie, moving everything onto one of them is still optimal, because the loss never looks at what was thrown away. (Real systems add a regularizer that stops the collapse from being total. It's a brake. The engine still pulls one way.)

So the oat-milk sofa is the candidate that won, under a system that gave the winner every seat. Averaging had nothing to do with it. The runner-up rooms, the ones with green velvet and terrible wallpaper, are probably still in the weights somewhere. They just never get called on.

The part that made me sit up was the fix. The same authors changed the objective to reward answers for being good and rare, and got about 75 percent more variety in stories and up to 46 percent more in invented personas, while winning head-to-head quality comparisons about as often as before. Which means the sameness is a default, the kind that stays put until somebody has a reason to change it.

Other groups have reached the same place from other directions. Take five models and compare each with its "aligned" chat version on a test of conceptual variety: alignment narrows every one of them, and none gets near the human baseline. Change nothing but the chat template, the role markers wrapped around your prompt, and variety drops anyway. And there's a finding that explains why switching vendors doesn't help, under the grand name of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (ICML 2024): as vision and language models get stronger, their internal representations converge on one another. Tolstoy would have recognised it. All strong models are alike; each weak model is weak in its own way.

So the honest version of my thesis is narrower than "AI averages culture," and I think worse: a handful of systems, finished by similar methods toward similar ratings, settle on the same winners, and then everybody draws their first draft from those winners. Tyler Cowen called his 2013 book Average Is Over. He was writing about the labour market. For the work itself I'd put it differently. The average isn't over. It's free, and nobody pays for what's free.

The study that got to me came out of Wharton in 2025, in Nature Human Behaviour. Five experiments on brainstorming with ChatGPT. In one, people had to invent a toy using a brick and a fan. With the chatbot's help the individual ideas got better, as they nearly always do. But 94 percent of them overlapped with somebody else's, and nine participants, working independently, gave their toy the same name: "Build-a-Breeze Castle."

Think about those nine people for a second. Each of them, as far as they knew, had named a toy. Each had seen one answer. Only the researchers saw nine.

Across the five experiments, the pool of ideas was narrower with ChatGPT in 37 of 45 comparisons. The most varied ideas in the whole study came from people using nothing but their own heads and a web search.

One lab could be a fluke. The meta-analysis is harder to wave away: 28 studies, 8,214 participants. People working with generative AI do somewhat better work than people working alone (effect size +0.27). The variety of ideas across those same people falls off a cliff (effect size −0.86, and in social science you rarely see a number that size with a minus sign in front of it). If you keep one sentence from this essay, I'd like it to be the next one.

That is also why it's so hard to notice. Your own work really did improve, and you have the evidence in front of you. The cost turns up somewhere you can't see from your desk. It turns up in the set.

You can hear it happening to the language. A 2025 paper in Science Advances went through 15.1 million biomedical abstracts looking for words whose frequency suddenly broke from its own trend. At least 13.5 percent of the abstracts published in 2024 carried a language model's fingerprints, and in some sub-fields 40 percent. "Delves" appeared 28 times more often than its history predicted. The authors counted 454 such excess words in 2024, against 190 at the height of COVID. By that measure a chatbot bent scientific English about twice as hard as a pandemic did.

Then it got out of the text box. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute analysed 824,634 podcast episodes, the unscripted kind, and found the same vocabulary climbing in human speech. ChatGPT's favourite words were rising 25 to 50 percent a year, and "delve" beat a synthetic control at p = 0.01. Nobody pasted those sentences. People said them, with their own mouths, because a model had said them first. Listen for it in your next meeting.

The pull has a direction, too. In a controlled study of 118 writers in India and the United States, the same autocomplete suggestions nudged the Indian writers toward Western conventions, in what they said and in how they said it, and gave them smaller productivity gains for their trouble. Autocomplete has an accent, and it probably isn't yours.

Now count the people in the room. About forty percent of American adults had used generative AI by late 2024. OpenAI claimed 800 million weekly users in October 2025. Ahrefs found machine-written text in 74 percent of newly published English web pages, though only 2.5 percent were machine-written from top to bottom. Radio, television and the feed all distributed culture after someone had made it. This is the first medium that hands out the first draft, to most of the people making things, at the same moment, from a handful of sources that agree with one another.

The web is the easiest place to watch this, because the web can be crawled.

It was converging long before the models showed up. A CHI paper from 2021 measured how visually different website layouts were from one another and found the distance had fallen 43 percent between 2010 and 2019. Blame the frameworks. Bootstrap sits under three out of four sites whose CSS framework can be identified, and Tailwind is downloaded 176 million times a week. The interaction designer Boris Müller had the diagnosis in 2018, in one line: templates are content-agnostic, and that's the problem.

Then the generators arrived and the sameness grew a face. You know this page. Inter, or the system font. A hero section, centred, under a small pill-shaped badge that says something like "Now in beta." A gradient running from indigo to purple. Three feature cards in a row, icon on top. Rounded corners, a shadow at ten percent opacity, shadcn components straight out of the box. You may have shipped this page. I'm in no position to judge.

In August 2025 Adam Wathan, who created Tailwind, posted a half-serious apology. Five years earlier he had picked bg-indigo-500 as the default button colour in Tailwind UI. The default was copied into so many tutorials that the models learned it as what a button looks like, and now it's the complexion of the machine-made web: one person's offhand choice, laundered through a training set into the taste of a generation of startups. When a parody site of vibe-coded landing pages reached the Hacker News front page, the top comment was two words long. Mode collapse.

In April 2026 the joke became a measurement. A developer named Adrian Krebs pointed a headless browser at 1,590 recent Show HN launch pages and ran sixteen deterministic checks for exactly these tells. Twenty-two percent of the pages had four or more. Another 32 percent had two or three. (He puts his false-positive rate at five to ten percent.) So more than half of the startups launching on Hacker News that spring wore at least two fingerprints of machine-made design, and they wore them on the one page where a company tries hardest to look like nobody else.

The benchmark followed in October. Fifteen frontier models, eighty design briefs, 2,400 generated interfaces. Every model scored above 90 percent on appropriateness, so these are not bad pages. But on how distinct different models' answers to the same brief were, the models scored 0.59 where human designers scored 0.76. On creative range, meaning how differently one designer handles different briefs, the models managed 0.58 against the humans' 0.90. Fifteen different AIs, asked for fifteen different apps, produced work more alike than human designers given the same brief. I should say that the authors build UI-generation tooling, so hold the decimals loosely. The direction matches everything else here.

Each page is fine. That's the trouble. The set is one page.

Kyle Chayka gave the look a name in 2016: AirSpace, the chain of near-identical cafés, co-working lofts and Airbnbs, all subway tile and reclaimed wood and Edison bulbs, in cities that have nothing else in common. His evidence was anecdote. The market's isn't. In 2017 Zillow went through 32,000 listing photos and found that a "greige" exterior sold for about $1,500 more than expected. In 2023 it surveyed 4,700 buyers and found that a dark graphite kitchen added roughly $2,500 while a white one cost you $600. Six years apart the winning colour was grey both times, pale and then dark. People were being paid to converge.

Nobody chose greige. Greige is what's left when everyone stops choosing.

Scale handles the rest. IKEA has sold more than 140 million Billy bookcases, which is more bookcases than America has households. In American cities one paragraph of the 2000 International Building Code, section 510.2, allowed five storeys of timber frame on a concrete podium, and the "five-over-one" became the skyline of every boomtown: 450,000 apartments finished in 2023 alone, nearly all of them to rent. When computer-vision researchers built a system in 2012 to tell cities apart from single Street View frames, it learned Paris, London and Barcelona easily. It couldn't find anything distinctive to learn about American cities.

Cars are the cleanest record of taste we have, because every sale is logged and every colour is something a person paid for. In more than 22 million US vehicle sales, the four non-colours (white, black, grey, silver) went from 47 percent of model-year 1996 cars to 80 percent of model-year 2025 cars. In 1996 one new car in 28 was grey. Now it's one in four. Worldwide, the paint maker Axalta has had the same four at around 80 percent year after year, and its 2025 report puts them at 81. These are a supplier's figures, with the caveats that implies, but you can check them in any car park.

An argument that can't say what would refute it is just a mood, so here is the best case against mine. It's better than I expected.

Fashion is the one domain someone has measured across more than 150 years of images, and it shows variety rising since the 1980s, with a crowd of niche looks replacing the single dominant one. Names went the same way: in 1955 American parents gave nearly a third of their sons a top-ten name, and by 2007 it was fewer than one in ten. National music charts on Spotify and iTunes drifted apart after 2017 when you'd have bet on them merging. People who take up streaming end up listening more widely than before. The genre map built from Spotify's own data counts more than 6,000 genres.

It gets closer to home. The collapse in human-AI work turns out to depend on the interface. When the model writes for you, variety falls. When it asks questions or offers options and the human stays in charge, quality goes up and variety holds; that's from a CHI 2026 study of more than a thousand people. Pay people for originality and the variety comes back, in two preregistered trials. The training collapse has a known fix. And the oldest result in this whole field, the MusicLab experiment of 2006, found that when its 14,341 participants could see each other's choices, hits became more unequal and less predictable. People herd, but where the herd ends up is close to a coin toss.

I accept all of it, and it narrows what I'm claiming. The free tier of everything becomes the same. The free tier is most of the volume. And the price of being visibly, legibly different from it goes up. Read that way, the counterexamples stop being exceptions. The niche label, the unusual name, the playlist somebody actually made: that's what the premium looks like when people pay it.

Back to the ladder. The Tail Premium says that when a technology compresses the middle of a distribution, the returns run to the ends. Everything above describes the compression, with one detail the first essay didn't have: the middle is crowded and it is also correlated. A million variations on one winner are one variation. So competence is no longer the scarce input, and "creativity" isn't quite it either, since the models do fine on individual originality. What's scarce is independence of source: an idea that didn't come from the same place as everyone else's.

The market already prices this, and the price has a shape. A 2025 paper in the Journal of Consumer Research scored 481,747 photos from New York Airbnb listings for visual uniqueness and matched them against occupancy. The curve was an inverted U. Listings that looked like every other listing were penalized. So were the truly strange ones. The best performers, by a margin worth thousands of dollars a year to a host, sat a measurable distance from the pack in a direction a guest could still read. That's the Tail Premium drawn as a curve: the rent goes to the room that is different on purpose and still makes sense, and the weirdest room does about as badly as the blandest. The grey car, seen this way, is a survey. It shows you where the margin went.

It also changes what a buyer can learn by looking. When artefacts converge, inspecting the artefact tells you less each year, and the question "who stands behind this, and what did they risk?" has to carry more of the weight. That's Human Signal. The number I expect to move is the Originality Premium, the price gap between work of verified origin and generated work in the same market, and it's the one I intend to measure.

What do you do about it on a Monday? I'm not going to tell you to stop using the tools. I won't, and you won't either. Using them costs you nothing. Accepting the first draft is the expensive part. So decide before you prompt: write down what you think, however badly, and only then ask. When you do ask for options, ask for twenty and bin the first five, because the first five are everybody's. And treat a model's defaults the way a decent cook treats a stock cube. Fine in an emergency. A confession on the menu.

The rule of this series is that an essay with nothing staked is an opinion in a nice jacket. So, three bets. They go on piszczek.pl/predictions with a commit hash before any of the windows open, each with a threshold, a deadline, a source that isn't me, and the outcome that proves me wrong. I've put a confidence on each, because I'd rather be calibrated than brave. If I say 80 percent and turn out right every time, I was sandbagging.

The third is the one I care about, so let me say it properly. Every era ends up named after whatever shaped its surfaces. We named most of a century after a queen and a decade after a school of design. We named a palette after a film stock and a face after an app. I think the 2020s get named after model families, because that's where most people making things drew their first draft. And I don't only mean pictures. A way of furnishing a room, a register of prose, a kind of chorus, a kind of face. People already say a poster looks "very Midjourney." The bet is that the habit leaves the trade and reaches things no model ever touched, until one day somebody describes a real kitchen, in a real house, with the name of a model, and everyone at the table knows exactly what they mean.

If these come in wrong, the essay was wrong, and I'll say so here in the same font size.

I don't know yet which of my friends will actually build the room in the render. Probably all of them, and I should be honest about why: it's a lovely room. That's how it won. It will photograph well, and nobody who visits will ever dislike it, which is a strange thing to be able to say about a place where a person lives.

So I'm not going to talk anyone out of the oak slats. If one of them asks, I'll say this, and I'll say it to you. Somewhere in the new place, keep one object that would lose every vote. Everybody owns one. The lamp from a grandmother's flat, in a colour that has no name. The chair that matches nothing. The painting a cousin made in a bad year. A model would never draw it, because no panel of raters would ever have agreed on it, and that's why it's worth more than the rest of the room put together. It's the only thing in there that couldn't have happened to anyone else.

Ask a machine what time is and you get a river. Ask it what home is and you get my friends' apartment. Tonight somebody, somewhere, is typing a warm, modern living room into a box, and the box is about to show it to them. They'll love it. They'll only ever see the one.

Scarcity never dies. It climbs. This time it climbed out of the product and into a smaller, odder question: whether the idea was yours before it was everyone's.

#9796. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9795. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9794. Dutch Police Arrest ‘Reformed’ Hacker in Shiny Hunters Investigation

Authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by the prolific hacker group ShinyHunters. In the days immediately following the suspect’s arrest, remaining ShinyHunters members dramatically escalated their attacks, stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the Russian ransomware group Cl0p.

According to three sources familiar with the matter, the Dutch man arrested by authorities this month is Pepijn van der Stap, a convicted cybercriminal from Almere and Lelystad in the Netherlands. Van der Stap was previously convicted in 2023 in connection with a string of data thefts and extortions that prosecutors said earned between €1.5 million and €2.7 million.

At his trial in late 2023, van der Stap admitted that he lived a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde existence, secretly using the hacker handle “Umbreon” to extort victims and post their data on English language hacking communities like the now-defunct RaidForums and Breached. By day, however, van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), a nonprofit security research group.

Pepijn van der Stap’s alter ego “Umbreon” selling a database on RaidForums, offering information on 2.3 million people from The Netherlands in September 2021. This user’s avatar is a depiction of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: KELA.

Van der Stap confessed to his data theft and extortion activity, and was sentenced to four years in prison (one of which was suspended). During his trial, van der Stap opted to remain in custody for a time rather than at home, saying he could not find better treatment on the outside for his ongoing psychological issues, which he claimed included PTSD related to childhood trauma. He was released from prison in December 2025.

In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, 2026, Van der Stap cast himself as a reformed hacker who was trying to turn his life around and make a positive contribution to society. Van der Stap is currently employed as offensive security lead at the Dutch company Neo Security, which did not respond to requests for comment.

Van der Stap said he was still dealing with civil lawsuits and restitution related to his previous cybercrime victims, and that he was trying his best to make amends. But not long after that interview, the Dutch hacker abruptly stopped replying to messages. Efforts by others close to him also repeatedly failed to elicit a response for the past two weeks.

The LinkedIn profile for Pepijn van der Stap.

According to two sources with knowledge of the matter, Van der Stap was arrested by Dutch authorities on or around September 16, and has been held in custody for questioning since. One source said a colleague of theirs personally witnessed Dutch authorities carting items out of Van der Stap’s residence.

Authorities in the Netherlands have been asking the public for help in identifying the voice in a recorded telephone call from February 2026 in which a native Dutch-speaking ShinyHunters member social engineered their way into Odido, the nation’s largest mobile telecommunications provider. In that intrusion, ShinyHunters tricked an Odido employee into logging in at a spoofed website, and then used that access to steal data on more than 6.2 million Dutch people.

Responding to Dutch news media, ShinyHunters confirmed that the suspect in the audio clip is indeed a member of the hacker collective.

“Our team member has our full support – emotionally, mentally, and financially,” the hackers said. “Everything has been arranged, including a criminal defense lawyer. We do not look down on our staff and members; we take excellent care of them,” reads a statement ShinyHunters shared with NL Times. It remains unclear if the Dutch police have matched the Odido caller to a confirmed real-life identity. The Dutch police unit handling the Odido incident did not respond to requests for comment.

The group also lashed out at the authorities in the Netherlands. “The Dutch police will need all the luck in the world – and everyone’s prayers – if they want to catch him before we carry out another large-scale data theft in the Netherlands,” the ShinyHunters statement said. “Frankly, the Dutch police are a big joke; they are incapable of doing anything. Incompetent. Irrelevant. Unimportant. Useless.”

Just days after sources say Van der Stap was detained by Dutch authorities, ShinyHunters claimed credit for an unusually brazen breach at the FBI’s job application site apply.fbijobs.gov. According to reporting from 404 Media, the data stolen from the FBI site includes Social Security numbers and personal information on more than 5,000 officials.

404 Media and Reuters reported the FBI data included each person’s job title or team, such as special agent, threat intake examiner, major cybercrimes unit, and those investigating cyber threats from foreign state-backed actors. Reuters examined documents shared by ShinyHunters and found they included sensitive psychiatric and medical files of FBI staff. The FBI issued a brief statement confirming the hack.

ShinyHunters said it gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a recently patched vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the software giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for the Peoplesoft vulnerability that ShinyHunters reportedly began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations who couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

But on Friday, BleepingComputer reported that ShinyHunters used a URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules designed to mitigate the threat from the PeopleSoft flaw. In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Van der Stap’s former hacker alias Umbreon was hidden in plain sight throughout the imagery ShinyHunters used to spread news about the FBI hack: The defacement image that ShinyHunters left behind on the hacked FBI jobs site included an ASCII art design featuring the Pokemon character Umbreon. The message at the top read, “This site has been seized by ShinyHunters. rooting your systems since ’19 ;)” The image appears identical to a defacement message ShinyHunters used in their 2020 hack of the English-language cybercrime community Hackforums.

The defacement message left by ShinyHunters on the FBI jobs site included an ASCII art rendition of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: Bleeping Computer.

Multiple sources close to the ShinyHunters investigation said the group’s recent risky attacks against the FBI and one of Russia’s most venerated ransomware groups amounted to a major pivot away from the more measured tenor of the hacking gang’s operations. Those sources said the sudden shift came about after ShinyHunters was taken over by a teenage cybercriminal from Amman, Jordan who goes by the nickname Rey and operates as part of a cybercrime group called ScatteredLapsussHunters (SLSH), which experts say is an amalgamation of three hacking groups — Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$ and ShinyHunters.

Those sources said Rey had an ongoing beef with the Dutch hacker over control of the ShinyHunters brand and data, and that the inclusion of the oversized Umbreon Pokemon image in the FBI jobs site defacement was likely an attempt by Rey to pin the hack on the Dutchman.

Rey was first publicly identified by the cybersecurity firm KELA in March 2025. In advance of our November 2025 profile of Rey, KrebsOnSecurity messaged Rey’s father and asked for permission to interview his teenage son. Rey’s dad merely forwarded the message to his son, who admitted to participating in ransomware attacks and said he was trying to extricate himself from the SLSH hacker group.

Immediately after news of the FBI jobs site hack was picked up in the media, Rey’s main account on Twitter/X (Ryan Moran/@rmoskovy) was taunting the Cl0p ransomware group and the FBI, crudely depicting them as the twin towers in New York being struck by planes labeled “cl0p drama” and “fbi breach claim.” In the foreground of the city is the giant Pokemon figure of Umbreon.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey’s now-defunct account on Sept. 22. A giant float-sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

On Sept. 24, KrebsOnSecurity again contacted Rey’s dad, asking to interview him and his son for a story on Rey’s apparent ascendency as the head of ShinyHunters. Just hours after that request, Rey deleted his longtime Twitter/X account. Meanwhile, Rey’s dad, who works for the Royal Jordanian Airlines, has failed to respond to a half-dozen emailed requests for comment about his son’s alleged activities.

Where does the bad blood between SLSH and ShinyHunters come from? According to a story in Wired this month, ShinyHunters and SLSH members briefly partnered earlier this year to help better monetize important stolen credentials collected by TeamPCP, an upstart group that was having great success compromising global code supply chains with malicious software but hadn’t been able to profit much from their stolen data (two alleged leaders of TeamPCP were arrested last month in Australia, and in an interview the TeamPCP leader claimed they made just $20,000).

The Wired story noted how Mandiant had infiltrated TeamPCP and was secretly responsible for having the crime group’s stolen credentials burned so quickly: Mandiant was secretly feeding those credentials to the major cloud providers like Amazon and Microsoft, who quickly invalidated the stolen keys. Meanwhile, the formerly cooperating hacker groups began to blame one another for causing the credentials to become worthless.

Wired’s Andy Greenberg reported that a few weeks after partnering with TeamPCP, “ShinyHunters went rogue, carrying out its own extortions with TeamPCP’s credentials but without giving the supply-chain hackers their cut.”

Mandiant researcher Austin Larsen told KrebsOnSecurity earlier this month that ShinyHunters has been enjoying a successful extortion spree so far this year, and is on track to pull in nearly $100 million in extortion payments from cybercrime victims in 2026.

Van der Stap claims he was never motivated by money and that his earlier hacker activity was driven by a desire to have the world’s most complete collection of stolen databases. Speaking with reporters from Bloomberg in 2024, Van der Stap said that singular focus in turn fueled his desire to carry out cyberattacks.

“The hacking was very easy for me, and it wasn’t a compulsion,” he told Bloomberg. “My habit was collecting. Collecting data, organizing data, downloading data, creating folders.”

DIVD, the nonprofit security research group where Van der Stap previously served as a volunteer, disclosed on LinkedIn last week that the organization was dealing with an internal cybersecurity incident that appears to have involved the malicious use of artificial intelligence. DIVD has released few details about that incident, but a spokesperson for the nonprofit told KrebsOnSecurity it does not appear related to ShinyHunters, nor are there any signs the matter involves the work of a previous volunteer.

Update: 3:44 p.m. ET: Corrected Van der Stap’s age, which is 24 (not 23).

Update, 4:54 p.m. ET: The Dutch police have confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. In a statement on Twitter/X, the Dutch police said the man will appear on Tuesday, September 29 before the chambers of the Rotterdam District Court, and that it will provide more information tomorrow.

Sept. 29, 9:42 a.m. ET: The Dutch news outlet RTL reports that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. RTL reported the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications the suspect gave the order for this.

The FBI released a short video message on the ShinyHunters investigation from Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI’s cyber division, who thanked Dutch law enforcement partners for their assistance and urged remaining ShinyHunters members to turn themselves in.

“Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk, and seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who’s left,” Leatherman said. “The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us, and we know how to find you. I suggest you reach out to us while the choice is still yours.”

#9793. What Memory Management Can Teach Us About Debt, Fiat Money, and Sustainability
