If you’ve written C++, you’ll probably know what manual memory management is. The following code is an example:

Of course, nowadays very few C++ programmers will still use raw pointers anymore, because it’ll easily lead to unnoticed memory leak, overlooked dangling pointers or unintentional double free, but it’s just an example showing some blind spots of those only knowing how to write programs in Garbage-Collected languages. While they might not ever need to manually manage memory, at least those writing codes for embedded systems and/or performance-critical software will be very hard to completely avoid manual memory management. Even for those lucky enough not having to manually manage memory, knowing how it works can still help writing codes in Garbage-Collected languages with higher performance, robustness and security, at least they can still be very vulnerable to the Out Of Memory error.

Consider the following code edited from some codes in a game engine, to show how circular reference can be an issue:

Let’s say every Battle object is recycled in a battle pool, and you’re playing a game where you can have multiple battles in distinct places all at once, in which you can choose which battle to focus on, causing the rest to be in real-time auto-battle. When all those battles end without starting any new battle, every Battle object will still hold a battler with its sprite, because actionBattler isn’t cleaned up yet until those Battle objects are reused in upcoming battles. This can be a problem if there are so many battles ending together without starting any new one, especially when it’s a 3D game, because a 3D sprite can consume a lot of memory, and obviously battles aren’t the only things that demand memory.

Actually, the problem can be a lot worse if it were a native iOS app, because both Objective-C and SWIFT still only use reference counting, causing all kinds of circular references to be vulnerable to memory leak. In this case, only actionBattler can still be theoretically freed, and the rest of the battlers along with their sprites will become massive memory leaks, because there are circular references among those battlers with their sprites. If a programmer doesn’t understand how memory management works, it’s only a matter of time before the game faces Out Of Memory errors.

To fix the memory leak issue, the following code can be added at the beginning of Battle.prototype.end:

The “weak” keyword can also be used in Objective-C and SWIFT, but programmers need to first know what it does.

Until now, “Download More RAM” is still just a sarcastic joke, but if one day, the internet connection speed becomes comparable with the M.2 SSD access speed, this can partially become a practical reality, even though it’d still be extremely risky. In the case of intranet, some computers might occasionally demand a lot of memory for a short time, then it’d be economical to have a single supercomputer connected to many workstations, and any workstation demanding lots of memory can temporarily download some virtual memory from that supercomputer. Or if you’ve some MMORPG servers being vulnerable to the Out Of Memory error, as long as those servers are located nearby some data centers with purely metered pricing on downloading virtual memory, this subscription can become the last line of defense. Bear in mind that, the physical downloading distance needs to be very close to make downloading memory really works, and in some cases, the most sophisticated remote direct memory access might already serve the purpose.

Actually, the distance limit due to the speed of light is just a small issue, because at least the downloaded memory can still be regarded as virtual memory using disk storage space, while the real danger is connection stability and security. It’s because now that some parts of the memory come from the internet, hackers would be a lot easier to access them, and once they’d such access, attacks like eavesdropping, privilege escalation, rootkit and man-in-the-middle attack can be done much easier and much more elusive than before. Without understanding how memory management works, if one day downloading virtual memory becomes feasible, those programmers might not realize the dangers it brings.

Alternatively, the data centers letting users download virtual memory might be down, or the internet connections could be down. Maybe it’s an accident, maybe it’s due to some hackers launching Distributed Denial-of-Services attacks, or maybe it’s just because the users somehow failed to pay for the purely metered pricing, but it really doesn’t matter. What really matters is that, if the programs accessing the downloaded virtual memory suddenly lose such access, what would happen to those programs, and those files accessed by them? While those files might have periodic backups to mitigate the risk of data corruption, programmers still need to understand memory management to know the risks.

On a side note: In the case of games, I’ve previously proposed an hybrid architecture that might replace cloud gaming decades later, because it’s built into the games right from the start. It causes the client side to just send raw inputs and configurations into the server side, with the server sending compressed and obfuscated rendering markups back to the client, while the rest will never leave the server. This completely eliminates all risks of downloading virtual memory or downloading any hardware capability in general, because in the case of games, cheaters will have to compromise the server before they can do anything, unless they’ve AI-based machine visions that are powerful enough to play for them while flawlessly disguised as a genuine human player, which is still very difficult when it comes to professional gaming.

Some programming languages like Kotlin can at least vaguely estimate how much memory it can still allocate from the system, as well as how much memory is needed to create an object, so such languages can sometimes avoid Out Of Memory by only creating objects when it’s likely that the system has enough memory for such memory allocations:

I’ve to admit that this implementation’s far from perfect, and it’s actually assisted by the AI I mentioned at the top of the article. While it’s prone to unlikely race conditions and it doesn’t accurately calculate whether there’s really enough memory for allocations, this example still aims to show another way when it comes to trying to avoid the Out Of Memory error. When tryAllocate is called, channel.send will take request as the argument, then processRequest will immediately be called with this argument taken. If the memory allocation is eventually successful, then successBlock will be called, otherwise failBlock will be called instead, so it basically applies the idea of promises into memory allocation.

However, even with the knowledge of promises, this doesn’t mean that programmers with no understanding on how memory management works can just use this example code as-is, it’s not just because of the aforementioned flaws, but also because of the implications of asynchronous memory allocations. In most GC languages, the traditional way of allocating memory is synchronous, meaning that it’s either a success or an Out Of Memory Error. But in the case of asynchronous memory allocation, the object to be created might be immediately created, created just before reaching the timeout, or never managed to be created at all. Myabe the failBlock will just call System.gc and then calling tryAllocate again, with the hope that the GC can really clean up enough memory for the upcoming memory allocations; Maybe the failBlock will try to instead create an alternate object as a poor man’s version, to hope that this time it’s be successful by demanding less memory; Maybe the entire object creation will be abandoned entirely, and a totally different business logic will be run instead. All these considerations demand knowledge of memory management.

In theory, when an object should’ve been created but it doesn’t exist yet due to not having enough memory for allocation, it can pretend that it’s already created. Then upon the 1st use of that object, if it doesn’t actually exist, that object will be created at that time, and then that already created object will be immediately used. One way to implement this is to use the option type, and the following oversimplified Kotlin code shows how this can be done:

Of course, if there are still not enough memory to create lazyBattler, the code will still throw the Out Of Memory error. Instead, the codebase needs to establish a centralized API using the idea of promises, so that upon calling a method of an object, object creation will try to take place. If it’s resolved, the method will be called immediately after object creation; if it’s rejected, some follow-ups will be done, maybe it’s a NOP, maybe an exception will be thrown, maybe it’s something else entirely. By using an object container to trace every object with its id, the following code can be used:

So the following code shows how callLazyMethod can be called, with methodBlock and successBlock being the focus:

In this case, successBlock needs the container to map the specified id to the created object, then immediately call the method block, which also needs to access the object via the container. If the code is run on servers being able to extend the hardware memory capacity on the fly, or download more memory from the internet/intranet on the fly, then such lazy objects can try to borrow memory from the future, even enough it’s still possible to throw the Out Of Memory error. Needless to say, this is pure insanity in most situations, but when I try to apply the wisdom of memory management in real lives, you’ll know that some seemingly normal operations are indeed this insane, assuming that you already understand memory management. But before that, I’ll have to talk about using hard disk space as virtual memory first.

Normally, when the physical memory is running out, the OS can swap some memory being least likely to be accessed frequently into some reserved portions of the hard disk, and these portions are the Swap Space. Although the fastest M.2 SSD being as fast as more than 14GB/s with 15us latency, is still nowhere comparable to the fastest DDR5-8600 being as fast as more than 130GB/s with 70ns latency, the former is still comparable to the deprecated DDR3-1600.

However, every SSD has a hardware limit called Terabytes Written(TBW), and once its limit’s exceeded, some portions of the SSD will start to become permanently read-only or even totally inaccessible, until no more data can be written into any part of the SSD. As M.2 SSD is of no exception, Swap Space should only be used as the last resort rather than the poor man’s real memory. Otherwise, even for M.2 SSD with TBW as high as 5600, frequently using a large amount of Swap Space will still drastically shorten the actual life span of M.2 SSD. Considering its price, this isn’t economical at all.

Consider a PC with 24x2GB DDR5-8600 and an 8TB M.2 SSD with 5600TBW and 16GB Swap Space, if apps frequently borrow lots of memory from the future, that 16GB Swap Space can be frequently accessed with lots of TBW used. Let’s say it’s as crazy as having 8TB I/O on the Swap Space per day on average, after 5600 / 8 = 700 days, which is nearly 2 years, the TBW will be fully used and the M.2 SSD will start to have problems. Needless to say, the expected lifespan of M.2 SSD of this caliber should be as long as 10 years or even more, so using it this way is a waste of precious resources. Bear in mind that, because of wear leveling, it’s not just the NAND flash in the Swap Space that will suffer, but actually the entire M.2 SSD will be slowly damaged, and almost no M.2 SSD will partition a Swap Space on the hardware level.

Not only that, since the latency of that M.2 SSD is 15us, while that of those memory is 70ns, such a drastic difference on the latency will lead to thrashing when the Swap Space’s frequently accessed with large amounts of data. It’s because major page fault is a lot more expensive than a minor one, and frequent access of the Swap Space will lead to lots of major page faults in a short time. If they also involve large amounts of data, then many pages of virtual memory will have to be mapped frequently into the page table as well, with the fact that those pages need lots of time to be created. Besides, lots of major page fault in a short time can lead to frequent context switching, which can constantly interrupt the I/O of the entire OS or even the hardware itself in extreme cases, so thrashing should never be taken lightly. After all, not all major OS have counterparts of ZRAM or ZSWAP, so borrowing memory from the future can be very dangerous.

The reason I have to explain these details is to show that, it’s really important for programmers to understand memory management, even if they’re just using Garbage-Collected languages only. For those only knowing how to write prompts for Generative AI to generate codes for them, without writing a single line of code themselves, the lack of understanding computer hardware can be even more disastrous. Also, since this article tries to apply some programming wisdom of memory management in real lives, you’ll have to understand memory management before reading the rest.

To avoid the Out Of Memory Error while allocating memory for every object, the following inequalities must be held:

M + S + D >= A >= A * (1 - F) * (1 - R) >= O * N * (1 - P)

S = the total amount of Swap Space from all M.2 SSD

D = the total amount of memory downloaded from the internet

F = the percentage of memory too fragmented to be allocated for creating any object

R = the percentage of memory allocation failed leading to resource starvation for the objects involved

O = the average amount of memory needed for object creation per object

N = the number of objects demanding memory allocation

P = the ratio of memory allocations for created objects being recycled in the object pool

There are 3 concepts not covered in this article yet – memory fragmentation, resource starvation and object pool:

Memory Fragmentation – It can be further divided into internal fragmentation and external fragmentation. Internal fragmentation will be a problem when there are lots of promises trying to asynchronously allocate memory for object creation, and this can be even more serious if those promises are also trying to borrow memory from the future. It’s because those promises themselves need to allocate small amounts of memory to be created, but if a memory page is 64KiB, lots of internal fragmentation will take place when many of those promises are created in a short time; External fragmentation can cause many objects that would’ve been created to fail to allocate enough contiguous memory, and this can eventually lead to many promises trying to create objects to be rejected instead. If many objects are created and destroyed in a short time, external fragmentation can quickly become very severe. Although both internal fragmentation and external fragmentation will be largely mitigated by the OS itself, and sometimes some Garbage-Collected languages can further help reducing internal fragmentation, both fragmentations will still be never trivial.

Resource Starvation – When memory allocation for object creation is performed asynchronously, it’s possible that some objects never managed to be created, causing the business logic needing those objects to be never run normally, ultimately causing other business logic having objects already created to throw exceptions as well. It’s especially the case when trying to borrow memory from the future, because the corresponding business logic doesn’t accept failure when first failing to create the objects needed, but rather gamble on the possibility that those objects can be created when they’re first needed. Such gambles are based on the anticipation that more physical memory will be added to the hardware on the fly, or more virtual memory will be downloaded from the internet, meaning that the whole architectural design’s the complete opposite of a fail-fast system, causing errors to be a lot harder to fix later on.

Object Pool – Let’s say you’ve a scrollable list having several hundred items, it’d be crazy to create every object for every item in the list right from the start, otherwise this can already cause the Out Of Memory error, or at least cause the list to take extremely long time to be loaded. Instead, all lightweight data of all items will be loaded into the memory in a lazy manner, but data like images will only be loaded while the corresponding items are currently displayed on the screen. Although frequent fast scrolling across lots of items will lead to frequent memory allocation and ultimately significant memory fragmentation, it’ll still better than loading several hundred images in the memory all at once.

Windows, MacOS and Linux are the 3 major OS in the PC market, but they handle the Out Of Memory error differently:

Windows – When Windows detects that the system’s about to be out of memory, it’ll first compress the least likely accessed memory pages to release some memory space, then it’ll start to use the reserved Swap Space if available memory is still tight, and finally rejects memory allocation requests from programs when there are still not enough memory. In very rare cases, where the memory demands of some programs cause the OS kernel to have insufficient memory in the non-paged area, the Windows might trigger BSOD to prevent permanently damaging the system itself.

MacOS – Similar to Windows, it’ll first compress the least likely accessed memory pages to release some memory space, as well as purging file caches and temporary data in memory, then it’ll start to use the Swap Space if available memory is still tight. But the difference is that, MacOS will keep extending the Swap Space until all SSD is used, only when they’re nearly full, restartable background services will be killed by Jetsam first, then users will have to manually kill some active apps if that’s still not enough. But if the thrashing’s too severe, it might cause a kernel panic instead.

Linux – Similar to MacOS, it’ll first recycle page caches to release some memory space, then it’ll start to use the reserved Swap Space if available memory is still tight. Users will either use ZRAM to compress the least likely accessed memory pages in the physical memory before using the Swap Space, or use ZSwap to compress those pages that’ll be in the SSD. If all these aren’t enough, the OS will call the OOM killer, which will assign oom_score to all apps consuming memory, and the ones with the highest scores will be forcibly killed by SIGKILL, but apps and services having root level access can set oom_score_adj to be -1000 to prevent themselves by being forcibly killed by the SIGKILL of the OOM killer.

The OOM killer in Linux deserves special attention here, because if many apps having severe memory leak set their corresponding oom_score_adj to be -1000, then the OS can still run out of memory even after the OOM killer kills all the other apps and services, which will cause the OS to have a kernel panic. Therefore, if some computer viruses managed to use privilege escalation to gain root level access, they can use their corresponding oom_score_adj to cause a kernel panic. While modern Linux won’t be so vulnerable to this attack vector, this vulnerability should still be taken seriously.

Sometimes it’s not the computer viruses that exploit this, but rather some legit apps borrowing memory from the future like crazy, by explicitly granting root access from users upon start, and using setuid to lower their access rights to its reasonable level after changing their corresponding oom_score_adj to -1000, the OOM killer will treat it as a normal user-level app that can’t be executed by SIGKILL. In contrast, some apps insisting on always synchronously allocate memory for object creations(thus being impossible to borrow memory from the future), might never touch their corresponding oom_score_adj, causing these apps not being the cause of OOM to be killed by the OOM killer instead.

With this much exploration on memory management, I can finally try to apply some wisdom there in real lives, and I’ll first talk about the essence of debt. When it comes to the raw pointers in C++, every new must be paired with exactly a single free, otherwise there will either be memory leak or double free; Similarly, for every debt involving a debtor and creditor, every borrowed debt must be repaid with the amount previously agreed upon, otherwise there will either be bad debt or risk of money laundering, usury, tax audit and frozen accounts, just like the risks caused by double free.

Viewing the essence of debt via promises, the creditor makes promises that the agreed amount will be disbursed to the debtor as a loan within the specified time interval, or the loan rejection logic previously agreed upon will be executed by the debtor; Similarly, the debtor makes promises that the borrowed amount will be repaid to the creditor within the specified time interval(the aspect of interests will be covered later), or the agreed logic of refusing to repay the debt will be executed by the creditor. Just as writing promises with only resolve but not reject is the anti-pattern of happy path coding(never handling any edge cases), making debt without exception handling is just asking for troubles.

Note that what people really need isn’t money itself, but rather the goods and services(including common goods and public services maintained by the government) that they can use money to buy from the market(or use tax to sustain the government). So disregarding the free-rider problem, when a debtor needs to borrow money from the creditor, it means that the debtor needs money to buy goods and services, but failed to produce goods and provide services with equivalent or higher market values. So the creditor will lend the loan only when he/she believes that the debtor is very likely to produce goods and provide services with market values higher than the loan amount before the loan expires.

When the creditor accumulates more and more bad debt due to the default of his/her debtors, the personal liquidity of that creditor will become smaller and smaller, eventually there will be so much bad debt that he/she won’t have any personal liquidity anymore, thus being unable to buy any needed goods and services. It’s like an app keep leaking more and more memory, until there are no more memory for that app to allocate for object creation, thus either throwing the Out Of Memory error or keep failing to run the needed business logic, eventually causing the app to cease functioning.

Before the adaptation of fiat money, money ultimately needs currently tangible entities as anchors, maybe they’re precious metal like gold, or maybe they’re a basket of daily necessities already on the market, but such anchors can never be anything in the future. On the other hand, fiat money doesn’t use any such concrete anchors, but rather use debt financing based on the national CPI and GDP to regulate the desired amount of M2, in order to avoid the problems caused by helicopter money, because now the central bank can use the policy rate to control the actual amount of M2.

Now that there’s debt involved, disregarding interest rates, those debt have to be eventually repaid, but the only way for the government to repay those debts is by tax and trade surplus in the future. However, when the scope is enlarged to the entire civilization, it’s the future tax of all governments in the world that keep repaying the debts necessary to keep fiat money working. The very fact that citizens are able to pay tax means that they’ve earned a lot more money than the tax they will pay, implying that they’ve produced goods and provided services of market value being much higher than the tax paid to the government. Therefore, the real anchors of fiat money are the goods and services that will be on the market in the future, forcing the civilization to keep producing more goods and providing more services than before, otherwise the debt will keep growing, until it’ll become so large that it’s impossible to repay anymore.

If physical memory corresponds to goods and services currently on the market, the Swap Space in the M.2 SSD corresponds to untapped natural resources pretending to the goods and services currently on the market, and the rest of the storage area in the M.2 SSD corresponds to obviously untapped natural resources, then the essence of fiat money becomes clear. In short, it’s just using asynchronous memory allocation to borrow memory from the future, based on the bet that more and more physical memory will be available on the fly, which is the same as the anticipation that the total amount of goods and services on the market will keep growing up in the future. In contrast, money using currently tangible entities as anchors strictly forbids asynchronous memory allocation, so it’s impossible for such money to borrow any goods and services from the future, meaning that any reckless object creation can lead to an instant OOM.

This can be easily illustrated by the 2008 financial crisis, ignoring the 50 trillion USD economic bubble vanished from the financial market, 19 trillion USD of global household wealth vaporized into thin air. On the other hand, how much worth of natural resources were destroyed? How much worth of goods were gone? How much worth of services were down? Probably nowhere near a trillion at most. This means that, even with a relatively conservative estimate, at least 18 trillion USD at that time were just promises of future goods and services, but never anything already materialized.

Nevertheless, fiat money does have its merits, provided that the central bank remain professional at all times. For instance, when the CPI increase rate is obviously too high or is noticeably higher than the GDP increase rate, if it’s because of having too much M2, then the policy rate can be increased to lower the CPI more than lowering the GDP, so that the excess M2 will first be collected by the commercial banks, then go back to the central bank. While the effects of such adjustments will be greatly diminished if the increase of CPI is due to lacking liquidity of goods and services, this shouldn’t occur so frequently. In fact, only the Russo-Ukrainian War and the 2026 Iran War have caused this recently.

Also, there might be some cases where some programs really need to borrow memory from the future, and I’ll use the following probably hypothetical example to show this. Let’s say you’ve a large server room having several server clusters, with each cluster having several servers as a single unit to run a unique app. In normal web traffic, a load balancer for each cluster will be enough, but when facing extremely large web traffic, if each customer request only needs a small data transfer object, while lots of memory needs to be allocated for creating objects to process them, synchronous memory allocation will either throw the Out Of Memory error, or have to deny some customer requests. Even with asynchronous memory allocation, if no memory’s borrowed from the future, some customers will still have to wait much longer than normal. Whereas if the app borrows memory from the future under this emergency, then immediately try to download memory from other server clusters, it’ll be possible that no customer have to wait for a very long time.

Recall that even M.2 SSD is still limited by its TBW, and if the Earth Ecosystem itself is the M.2 SSD of the civilization, then the rate of writing data shouldn’t be much higher than normal usage, otherwise the lifespan of the M.2 SSD will be a lot shorter than expected. However, if the M.2 SSD is mainly used as the Swap Space, then it’s almost certain that the rate of writing data will soon become ridiculously high, causing the M.2 SSD to degrade unusually quickly. While the Earth Ecosystem can recover itself if it’s given enough time to rest, this is basically no longer the case once the civilization advanced into industrial revolution. Loosely speaking, industrial revolution allowed the civilization to extract natural resources much faster than before, thus upgrading the hard disk from HDD to SSD, making Swap Space to become somehow practical. As technologies kept advancing, the SSD was then further upgraded into the M.2 SSD.

To investigate further, let’s try to do some math using numbers given by the AI I mentioned at the top of this article:

1.       The current sustainability limit of the Earth Ecosystem is 12.3 billion GHA

2.       The current annual GHA consumed by the civilization is 22 billion GHA, causing 22 – 12.3 = 9.7 billion GHA permanent damage to the Earth Ecosystem annually

3.       The theoretical annual GHA consumed by the civilization could be 60 billion without caring the sustainability of the Earth Ecosystem, this can be reached if the civilization keeps insisting on needing infinite exponential growth

4.       If the annual GHA consumed by the civilization is still 22 billion for the next 60 years, the Earth Ecosystem will become unable to sustain the civilization anymore, causing the civilization to completely collapse

5.       Combining 2 and 4, the remaining “TBW” of the Earth Ecosystem can be roughly estimated to be 9.7 billion GHA * 60 years = 582 billion GHA

6.       Combining 3 and 5, the most pessimistic estimate of the remaining life of the civilization = 582 / (60 – 12.3) = 12.2 years

While these are just rough estimates rather than accurate calculations, and I don’t think the civilization will suddenly become insane enough to throw away its sustainability altogether, the point is still to show that, even the Earth Ecosystem itself does have its TBW limit once its sustainability limit’s exceeded by the civilization, so the point is to try to reduce the annual GHA consumed by the civilization to be way below 12.3 billion GHA before the civilization collapses. However, it’s possible that the sustainability limit of the Earth Ecosystem will drop below 12.3 billion GHA if it’s still being constantly damaged by the civilization, so 60 years being the most optimistic estimate can be overly optimistic.

As technologies keep advancing, the civilization keeps creating more and more technofossil that further damages the Earth Ecosystem, and keeps forcing more and more species to be extinct, thus threatening the biodiversity of the Earth Ecosystem. Because the wear leveling algorithms of both the Earth Ecosystem and the civilization are too weak to evenly distribute the damage across the whole world, and the reasons for the civilization to damage the Earth Ecosystem is to quickly extract lots of resources and swiftly dispose lots of wastes, the more developed areas are usually more damaged too. But since the civilization treats the ocean as its rubbish bin, some undeveloped areas also suffer from those wastes.

If these were like writing data into the M.2 SSD, it’s not only that some portions become read-only, but also that some other portions are overwritten by poisonous data that corrupt some other data in some other portions that need to read those portions being overwritten by those poisonous data. For instance, when the Pacific Ocean are filled with more and more marine debris, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch began to form, thus damaging the nearby ecosystem, causing more and more marine lives dying, more and more seafood being poisoned, and even slightly enhancing the global warming. Another example is the Amazon Rainforest, which is already significantly damaged, has been changed from a carbon sink to be a carbon source, thus further contributing to the greenhouse effect. Not only that, the flying river above the Amazon Rainforest might be eventually blocked, thus changing the rainfall patterns of South America. This can be another source of an unforeseen butterfly effect, because the Earth Ecosystem has lots of unknown chaotic properties.

Before globalization, as long as a nation can produce goods and provide services domestically, it’d be sometimes more effective and efficient than relying on other nations that are very far away from itself. But since globalization drastically increased the effectiveness and efficiency of traveling from anywhere to anywhere else, it’s like raising the internet connection speed to be comparable to the M.2 SSD access speed, causing downloading natural resources, goods and services from other nations to become much more economical. Strictly speaking, there are many kinds of memory in the civilization, because its professions become so specialized that almost no nation can run the entire supply chain all by itself. This is the direct result of swift technological advance, causing the supply chain to be very complex and colossal.

For instance, nation A is uniquely good at producing computer chips, nation B is uniquely good at producing and maintaining ULCV needing those chips, nation C is uniquely good at producing crops and livestock, nation D is uniquely good at processing rare-earth mineral, nation E has overwhelming rare-earth mineral reserves… Almost all developed nations need all these goods and services and many more others to keep running, but none of them can produce and provide them all domestically, so they’ll have to download all kinds of memory from many other nations via the internet based on globalization. If there are severe transportation problems between nation D and E, nation E can fail to effectively and efficiently deliver lots of rare-earth mineral to nation D, causing nation A to fail to get enough ingredients from nation D needed for running the computer chip factories, further causing nation B to fail to keep producing and maintaining ULCV for nation C, ultimately causing many nations to fail to import enough crops and livestock in time.

While this is just a hopefully made-up example, just take a look on how Ever Given once shortly crippled the entire just-in-time global supply chain with Suez Canal as a single point of failure(SPOF); alternatively, Strait of Hormuz is probably another SPOF, where 20% of petroleum needed to use it to be exported across the world. When a system with multiple distributed modules has multiple SPOF, it’ll be reasonable to suspect that it’s actually a Distributed Monolith, even though further investigations will be needed to confirm this suspicion. In short, Distributed Monolith combines most of the disadvantages of monolithic application and Distributed Microservices, while having almost none of their advantages, meaning that it’s one of the worst anti-patterns possible, and should always be avoided like a deadly plague.

I don’t know if anyone has already published the dependency graph of all the major natural resources, goods and services across every major nation in this world, but if almost no one in the civilization can draft this, this is equivalent of developing a codebase with hundreds of billions of lines of code but without any solution architect nor even systems analyst. I previously stated the danger of programmers not understanding memory management, especially when they’re using Generative AI to generate codes for them without even reading those code first, but if those influencing the global supply chain don’t understand it or don’t know how the Earth Ecosystem works, it’ll be same level of danger.

Now let’s try to do some other math about money using numbers given by the AI I mentioned at the top of this article:

1.       The current worth of all natural resources known to be usable by the civilization is 500 trillion USD

2.       The current worth of all goods and services on the market is 128 trillion USD measured by the total GDP

3.       The total debt of the civilization is 313 trillion USD

4.       The average compound interest rate of the debt from all fiat money is 4.59%

5.       The upcoming compound interest of the civilization debt is 313 trillion * 4.59% = 14.3 trillion USD, which is 14.3 / 128 = 11.2% of the current worth of all goods and services on the market measured by the total GDP

6.       If both the base total debt and its average compound interest rate remains unchanged, after (log500 - log313) / log1.0459 = 10.4 years, the total debt will be the worth of all natural resources, without considering inflation

Since the goods and services are produced and provided by the citizens, and they’ve to do so to earn money, it means that 11.2% of their income will have to repay the debt as an indirect tax. Then how exactly fiat money levy indirect taxes from the citizens? It’s impossible to be merely inflation, because the average amount of inflation of the civilization is just 4.7%, meaning that the remaining 11.2% – 4.7% = 6.5% must have been collected by some other ways. The answer is shrinkflation of goods on the market, where its average amount across the civilization is 12.5%, meaning that the remaining 12.5% - 6.5% = 6% becomes the profit of the goods producers. Since they need to pay taxes to the government, their increased gross and net profit will force them to pay more taxes. While I failed to find the amount of shrinkflation of services on the market, and I hope it won’t be high, it doesn’t seem to be much better either.

Recall that the real anchors of fiat money are the goods and services that will be on the market in the future, but now with the average compound interest rate of its debt being 4.59%, it means that the annual compound growth of the total worth of all goods and services currently on the market needs to be more than 4.59%. However, without more than 4.59% of the compound growth of the total demand of the civilization, excess capacity will become a problem of fiat money, and the current amount of excess capacity is 22%. Not only that, because the annual compound growth of the amount of extracted natural resources is 2.3%, it means that their utilization need to be at least 1.0459 / 1.023 – 1 = 2.2% more effective and efficient in a compound manner, meaning that technological advances need to have compound growth as well. So, the whole civilization needs to sustain compound growth, just to sustain the fiat money.

Since the adaptation of fiat money in 1971, even though the global population right now(8.3 billion) is more than a double than before the adaptation(3.8 billion), the increase rate of global population is actually decreasing, from 2.06% annually to 0.84% annually. But because the fiat money keeps running until now, it means that the compound growth of the total demand of the civilization managed to keep up with the average compound interest rate of the debt from all fiat money. Therefore, the annual compound growth of the average demand per person right now must be more than 1.0459 / 1.0084 – 1 = 3.7%, and such growth, when accumulated over the years, can severely harm the mental health.

All these only make fiat money worse than borrowing memory from the future, because memory allocation doesn’t have interest rate, but if there were no interest rate of fiat money based on debt, who’ll be willing to disburse the loan? It means that interest rate is necessary for fiat money to work, and any attempt of simple interest will most likely degrade into compound interest over the years, simply by maliciously abusing trailing twelve months to recalculate the principal of the simple interest every month. Let’s say the annual simple interest rate of fiat money is 3%, then the monthly counterpart would be 0.25%, but if the old debt needs to be repaid monthly, and the principal of the new debt increases by 0.25%, the effective annual interest rate will be 1.0025 ^ 12 – 1 = 3.04% as a compound interest instead.

Recall that fiat money is just using asynchronous memory allocation to borrow memory from the future, and promises will be used to implement this, but since those promises themselves also need to allocate small amounts of memory to be created, this will become a problem when combined with compound interests. As mentioned, lots of promises each allocating a small amount of memory can lead to severe internal memory fragmentation, meaning that the actual amount of memory consumption by those promises themselves can be noticeably more than their own sizes. This implies that, for every loan disbursed by the creditor to the debtor, there will be nontrivial transaction costs associated with it. While its average of the central bank is just 0.05% of the debt, since the total amount is 313 trillion USD, the accumulated transaction cost over the years is still 156.5 billion USD; In the case of the market borrowing money from commercial banks, the average transaction cost is 2% of the total debt, which is 220 billion USD out of 11 trillion USD.

The majority of such transaction costs come from the reserve requirement for every commercial bank from the law, and this law wouldn’t exist if the anchors of money were currently tangible entities, since asynchronous memory allocation would be impossible. But in the case of fiat money, the maximum number of concurrent promises, as well as their retry and timeout intervals, all needs to be regulated by the central bank via the policy rate and the amount of the reserve requirement, all according to the current amount of physical memory and its predicted amount in the future.

To avoid running out of natural resources while keeping everyone alive, the following inequalities must be held:

N – T >= E >= E * M * S >= D * P * (1 - R)

N = the total recovery rate of all natural resources without any damage done by the civilization

T = the total damage rate of the Earth Ecosystem including those done by technofossil

E = the total extraction rate of all natural resources

M = the average effectiveness and efficiency of converting natural resources into goods and services on the market

S = the average supply and demand match rate of all goods and services on the market

D = the average total demand of a person across everyone

R = the average reuse and recycling rate of all sold goods and services

According to the AI I mentioned at the top of this article, the current numbers of these variables are the following:

1.       The inequalities become 12.3 billion GHA >= 22 billion GHA * 33% * 90% >= 2.9 GHA * 8.3 billion * (1 – 7%)

2.       This leads to 12.3 billion GHA >= 6.5 billion GHA >= 22.4 billion GHA, suggesting that (22.4 - 6.5) / 22.4 = 71% of the global population isn’t covered by comprehensive social protection. Also, 42% of the global population’s facing the lack of infrastructure, and they probably aren’t covered by comprehensive social protection either, meaning that 29% of the global population have the infrastructure but don’t have comprehensive social protection.

3.       This includes the fact that N – T = 12.3 billion GHA < E = 22 billion GHA, leading to a 22 – 12.3 = 9.7 billion GHA permanent damage to the Earth Ecosystem annually, causing T to keep increasing, until it becomes close to N.

Of course, with better technologies combined with improved economic and political systems, M, S and R will increase, but none of them will ever reach 100%, at least because of the 2nd law of thermodynamics. According to the AI I mentioned at the top of this article, the practically maximum possible values of M, S and R are 68%, 98% and 25% respectively in the future. Assuming that these are the current numbers instead, the inequalities become 12.3 billion GHA >= 22 billion GHA * 68% * 98% >= 2.9 GHA * 8.3 billion * (1 – 25%), leading to 12.3 billion GHA >= 14.7 billion GHA >= 18.1 billion GHA. While the reality would become much better already, the inequalities still don’t hold at all.

I previously established that, because of the 4.59% average annual compound interest rate of all fiat money in the civilization, with the 0.84% annual global population increase rate, the average annual exponential growth of the demand per person needs to be more than 3.7%, otherwise excess capacity will cause the fiat money to fail to sustain the ever increasing debt. However, as more and more young generations in most of the major nations embrace the anti-hustle culture, especially in the forms of tang ping, simple living and quiet quitting, the average total demand of a person begins to drop from the peak since 2010s partially because of these practices, and they also partly causes the global population to be predicted to reach the 10.3 billion peak in 2080s before dropping. Combining these effort, D * P in the inequality should reach its peak soon before starting to drop, thus buying more time for more permanent solutions.

One of the very reasons the old generations are so offended by the anti-hustle culture rapidly spreading across the young generations is that, if the total demand of the civilization drops too quickly for too long, the economic bubble called fiat money might be popped before the old generations dies, which will likely destroy their entire lifestyles over the past decades. This means that, their current lives are partly sustained by the effort of the young generations keeping exponential growth of the demands of goods and services on the market, thus helping the fiat money to sustain its debt with compound interests, implying that the civilization has already partially become a Ponzi Scheme.

Theoretically, it might be possible to find the optimal amount of the adaptation of the anti-hustle culture, such that the civilization can perform a soft landing without popping the fiat currency bubble before the old generation dies, but needless to say, even if such an amount does exist in reality, it’s almost impossible for the civilization to accurately calculate its value, let alone controlling itself to strictly regulate that amount to keep being that value. Therefore, the aforementioned generation gap caused by the fiat money will only keep increasing as the debt keeps increasing, and loosely speaking, the amount of debt of the civilization is a rough estimate of the amount of the generation gap.

Now let’s assume that everyone in the civilization suddenly understands the Civilization Sustainability Inequalities, causing them to recognize the Ponzi Scheme run by the fiat money, what would the old and young generations do respectively? I can foresee that real property, public pension system, as well as the debt of the fiat money itself being the hot potato, will be some of the major battlefields among these generations. Actually, there are already such battles, but with the truth revealed to them all, these battles will ironically become even fiercer, since the fig leaf’s gone now. Therefore, the optimal strategy for the young generation might be actively proclaiming the Civilization Sustainability Inequalities among itself, while letting the old generation fiercely deny the truth of natural resource management.

Since I don’t want this article to be all criticisms without suggestions, I’m going to propose an alternative, with the core idea that money should’ve currently tangible entities as anchors most of the time, with fiat money as state of emergency. A more detailed outline, though still oversimplified, will show how this can be put into action in the future:

1.       Normally, the official data of the amount of electricity generated, essential goods produced and necessary services provided, as well as the precious metal storage, over the last quarter, should form a weighted basket as the anchor of money for the next quarter

2.       The calculations of the weights of the elements in the basket, as well as the policy rate for the next quarter, should consider the quarter CPI, GPI(rather than GDP), and the data of those elements, as well as their Year-to-Year and Quarter-to-Quarter counterparts, such calculations need to follow a system that’s publicly disclosed

3.       While the government can declare state of emergency to let the central bank use the fiat money, the national legislature can apply a judicial review in the Supreme Court, which has the right to stop the state of emergency

Needless to say, lots of details will have to be heavily refined, or corruptions will soon degrade this system into something much worse than pure fiat money. For instance, excess capacity of electricity, goods and services need to be subtracted from the data used as the anchor of money, or it’ll only encourage and recommend involved stakeholders to keep increasing excess capacity; the system calculating the weights of the elements in the basket as well as the policy rate need to be objectively verifiable by civilian AI, independent economists and other major nations; the aforementioned judicial review needs to cause the supreme court to temporarily halt the state of emergency if the national legislature managed to establish a prima facie case after a week, before the central bank has a case to answer; if the judgment of the Supreme Court shows that the government is intentionally abusing the state of emergency, then the national legislature can use this judgment to impeach the president of the government. There are obviously a lot more bugs to be fixed and tests to be added to make this system work, but these are just some obvious examples.

Actually, all these are just tactical challenges, with some of them being almost impossible to overcome, but the real problems are the strategic disasters my suggestions will probably bring to nations trying to implement this, which is Gresham’s Law as a result of the prisoner’s dilemma. First, to probably implement my system without persistently severe corruptions, data transparency as legal requirements is a must, but since I’m talking about the amount of electricity, essential goods and necessary services, forcibly exposing these data can threaten national security for major nations; Second, if some major nations managed to implement my system properly, while some other nations insist on using pure fiat money, what will happen to those nations using my system? Third, it can be easily foreseen that, being able to implement this system implies that the young generation has the majority of votes, because it’s just unthinkable for the old generation to support my system, but then the generation gap will only be worsen by my system; Finally, some politicians will eventually take the extreme risks and intentionally create external conflicts and internal crisis just to justify the use of the fiat money, and the supreme court might not be fast enough to stop this before it’s too late.

This means that, the only way for my system to become the reality is that, every major nation has to implement them at the same time, with International Monetary Fund and United Nations as their economical and political supervisors respectively. Needless to say, it’s nearly impossible right now, but even when many years have passed, and most citizens in the civilization understands that the fiat currency bubble is about to burst, I still highly doubt if the civilization will suddenly become this united, because some politicians will always stick to “Après moi, le déluge”.

The 2008 financial crisis vanished 50 trillion USD of pure bubble, which is essentially a giant island of circular references not ultimately reachable by already existing goods and services on the market as the Garbage Collection Root, meaning that those derivatives should’ve been deleveraged by escape analysis right from the start, or at least repriced by tri-color marking before the bubble’s popped. While economic bubble can still exist without the fiat money, the sheer amount of 50 trillion USD should’ve proven that it can quickly enlarge such bubble into uncontrollable levels; the COVID-19 pandemic had forced the civilization to temporarily stop exponential growth for nearly 3 years, meaning that it’s actually capable of at least reducing its total GDP growth into 4.3% from early 2020 to early 2023, resulting in an average of annual 1.4% GDP growth during that period. These 2 events showed that the civilization not only understands the dangers of the fiat money, but is also able to replace the exponential growth with a more sustainable growth curve.

Back in 1971, when the gold standard can’t sustain the economic growth of the civilization anymore, quite some renowned economists suggested systems much better than what I’ve suggested here. But because the technologies back then were nowhere as advanced as now, those alternatives weren’t even technically feasible, forcing the fiat money to be the new norm. The problem is, although we already have technologies needed to run the alternatives, the civilization has become so addicted to the fiat money that, even Methadone-like alternatives won’t be considered.

#9792. ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests

A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”

A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”

Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.

However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey, his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees.

Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.

Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.

Rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today.

Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.

Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors said netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.

Neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der ⁠Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.

A screenshot of a Sept 16 story by the Dutch news outlet at5.nl, describing a police raid on Van Der Stap’s residence that reportedly used flash-bang grenades.

Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.

When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.

“You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”

Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.

More to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.

In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.

“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make new Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.

A relatively new Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

“Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”

In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”

#9791. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9790. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.
